# Twyne tools `@twyne/tools` provides two local, scriptable ways to work with a Twyne account: - `twyne`, a CLI for authentication, folios, critiques, and citations. - `twyne-mcp`, a stdio MCP server with exactly 10 focused tools. Both clients use Twyne's authenticated `POST /api/integrations/v1` boundary. The access token belongs to the local user and is never sent anywhere except the configured Twyne URL. The package also exposes local Codex and Anthropic SDK adapters. They are separate from Twyne account authentication: each adapter reuses the credential owned by its provider's official CLI. ## Install and authenticate Requires Node.js 20 or newer. ```sh npm install --global @twyne/tools twyne auth login --url https://YOUR-TWYNE-DEPLOYMENT ``` Paste the personal access token at the hidden prompt, pass it with `--token`, set `TWYNE_ACCESS_TOKEN`, or pipe it on stdin. Login validates the token before saving it. The saved config lives at `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/twyne/config.json` (normally `~/.config/twyne/config.json`) and is created with mode `0600`; its directory is mode `0700`. `TWYNE_CONFIG_PATH` can select another config file. For ephemeral environments, skip the config file: ```sh export TWYNE_API_URL=https://YOUR-TWYNE-DEPLOYMENT export TWYNE_ACCESS_TOKEN=twyne_pat_... twyne auth status ``` The environment variables must be supplied together and take precedence over the config file. ## Provider SDK sign-in Install the SDK you intend to use, then sign in through its official local CLI: ```sh npm install @twyne/tools @openai/codex-sdk @anthropic-ai/sdk twyne provider login codex twyne provider login anthropic twyne provider status codex twyne provider status anthropic ``` Codex opens the ChatGPT sign-in flow and stores its own credential. Anthropic delegates to `ant auth login`, which creates an Anthropic profile consumed by the SDK. `twyne provider logout codex|anthropic` delegates sign-out to the same official CLI. # Optimizing prompts with `prompt-learning`

`evals/optimize_prompts.py` runs the
[vendored `prompt-learning` SDK](../tools/prompt-learning/TOOLS_PATCHES.md)
against one of our `.md` prompt files. The wrapper supplies a Not Organic
provider and accepts the hosted text aliases `fast`, `balanced`, and `reasoning`.
The shared TypeScript client handles assertion exchange, DPoP, metering and
idempotency; the Python provider reserves the approved per-call ceiling.

## One-time setup

```bash
python -m venv .venv-prompt-learning
.venv-prompt-learning/bin/pip install -e tools/prompt-learning
```

## Selecting a target

The first prompt to optimize is the one whose failures you can actually
describe in plain words — `integrity-judge-system` and
`citation-format-system` are good first targets because each has a
specific failure surface and a single, attributable judge model in
`evals/judge.ts`. The room-of-editors `persona-system` is the
biggest-blast-radius target but also the slowest to converge because
its failures spread across all five personas.

## CSV shape

The driver expects a pandas-shaped CSV with at least:

- an `output` column: the model's previous output for that case
- a `feedback` column: free-form natural-language feedback for each row
  (why the output was wrong, what was missing, etc.)
- any other columns whose names appear as `{vars}` in the `.md` body

Twyne's existing eval JSONL files (`evals/rubric.jsonl`, etc.) get
reshaped into this format by hand or with a tiny TS pre-step that joins
the eval output with `rubric-scores.json` and emits a CSV.

## Run

```bash
# dry-run: load + parse everything, skip the optimizer (no API call)
bun run prompts:optimize:dry -- --prompt integrity-judge-system \
    --csv evals/datasets/integrity-judge.csv --model reasoning

# Real run: load Not Organic assertion settings, TWYNE_EVAL_DID, and an
# approved TWYNE_EVAL_MAX_COST_MICROUSD from your protected secret store.
# See README.notorganic.md. No upstream key belongs in this tool.
python evals/optimize_prompts.py --prompt integrity-judge-system \
    --csv evals/datasets/integrity-judge.csv --model reasoning --budget 2.00
```

The driver writes `prompts/integrity-judge-system.md.new` (not in place)
so you read the diff before swapping:

```bash
diff -u prompts/integrity-judge-system.md prompts/integrity-judge-system.md.new
mv prompts/integrity-judge-system.md.new prompts/integrity-judge-system.md
bun test  # verify regression tests still pass
```

## Cost guardrails

`--budget` is a required USD ceiling for a live run. The subprocess provider
reserves the entire `TWYNE_EVAL_MAX_COST_MICROUSD` before every logical call,
including uncertain failures. This conservative accounting may stop before
actual charges reach the run ceiling. The gateway separately enforces wallet
access and the per-call ceiling. Failed or incomplete runs do not stage a prompt.

## Inspecting candidate quality

The optimizer returns the candidate it liked best under its internal
Agent → Evaluator → Meta-Prompt loop. It's not always an improvement; it
is _always_ a candidate. The decision to take it is yours, in the diff
review. Treat the output as "a colleague proposed this", not "the system
decided this".

## Updating the SDK

Preserve the custom provider injection interface and run the offline contracts
when updating the vendored SDK. See `TOOLS_PATCHES.md` for the integration and
`README.notorganic.md` for server-only configuration.

/**

 * "audience · goal" context, and a set of candidate sources — each pre-labelled
 * `relevant: true|false` as ground truth. For every candidate, we ask the LLM

/**
 * TARGET-EXTRACTION eval for Twyne's Apparatus.
 *
 * `run-apparatus.ts` scores the step *after* search: given a query and a
 * candidate source, is the source relevant? This scores the step *before* it —
 * the one the writer actually feels. Given a draft, does the extract pass flag
 * the passages that must be checked, and leave alone the ones that must not?
 *
 * Two things make this eval worth trusting:
 *
 *   1. **It runs the shipped prompt.** The system and user bodies come from
 *      `src/utils/research-targets.ts`, which renders the same `prompts/*.md`
 *      files the app ships, and the reply is parsed by the same
 *      `parseResearchTargets`. An edit to the markdown moves this score. A
 *      hand-copied template in the harness would not.
 *   2. **Scoring is deterministic — no judge.** Each case names the passages
 *      that must be flagged and the passages that must not, each identified by
 *      needles that have to appear in a target's anchor or query. There is no
 *      second model to be biased, so a regression is a regression.
 *
 * Reads `evals/extract.jsonl`; writes `evals/extract-scores.json`.
 *
 * Metrics:
 *   recall        — required passages that got a target  (misses = under-flagging)
 *   false_flag    — forbidden passages that got a target  (noise the writer sees)
 *   kind_accuracy — of matched targets, how many carried the expected kind
 *   mode          — dossierResearchMode() vs the expected mode (no API call)
 *
 * Env: Not Organic eval configuration (see evals/README.notorganic.md). The mode check runs without it.
 */

  buildDossierResearchInstructions,
  buildResearchExtractSystemPrompt,
  buildResearchExtractUserPrompt,
  dossierResearchMode,
  parseResearchTargets,
} from "../src/utils/research-targets";

=== evals/run-local-model.ts
/**
 * Tool-calling + analysis eval for a small local model (e.g. LFM2.5-2.6B),
 * the candidate engine for signed-out / free mode.
 *
 * Every other script in `evals/` talks to the Not Organic gateway with a
 * bare system+user body and never passes `tools`. None of them can answer the
 * only question that matters for a 2.6B on-device model: *can it drive the
 * `quote_passage` tool?* That tool is what pins an editor's note to a real
 * passage; a model that cannot call it produces unanchored notes, which is a
 * different (worse) product, not a slightly weaker one.
 *
 * So this script runs the REAL production path rather than an approximation:
 * the prompts from `convex/agentPrompts`, the tool from `convex/agentTools`,
 * `generateText` with `stopWhen: stepCountIs(3)` exactly as
 * `src/utils/ai-client.ts` does. What it changes is only the endpoint.
 *
 * Two runs per case, so tool competence and analysis competence are separable:
 *   - `tools`   — the real path, with `quote_passage` offered.
 *   - `notools` — same prompts, no tool. The control. If analysis is fine here
 *                 and collapses in `tools`, the tool is the problem, not the
 *                 model's reading of the draft.
 *
 * Output is written to two places:
 *   - `evals/local-model-scores.json` — per-case tool metrics + the aggregate.
 *   - `evals/local-model-runs.json`   — `{case_id, output}[]`, the exact shape
 *     `evals/judge.ts` reads. Copy it over `evals/runs.json` and run
 *     `bun run eval:judge` to score analysis quality against the same
 *     faithfulness/helpfulness rubrics used for the hosted models, so the
 *     small model is compared on the incumbent's terms.
 *
 * Serving the model — anything OpenAI-compatible works. llama.cpp needs
 * `--jinja` or it will not emit tool calls at all:
 *   llama-server -hf LiquidAI/LFM2.5-2.6B-GGUF --jinja -c 8192
 *
 * Usage:
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080/v1 bun run eval:local
 *
 * Env:
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_BASE_URL  default http://localhost:8080/v1
 *   LOCAL_MODEL_ID        default LFM2.5-2.6B

I'm noting these Convex actions need an authenticated user and linked DID, with a legacy provider fallback when that's disabled, and now I'm weighing how an external CLI or MCP tool could actually drive this real application harness for evals—starting with the option of calling the Convex actions directly over some transport.

Going through the HTTP client path, I realize calling actions like `runPersona` requires a JWT-based identity from `ctx.auth.getUserIdentity()`, but personal access tokens used by the integrations API aren't JWTs, so identity wouldn't propagate through an httpAction's internal calls—meaning I'd likely need internal variants that take an explicit owner identifier instead of relying on ambient auth. The alternative is running the actual harness logic in-process by importing the same underlying functions the Convex actions use, bypassing the auth-dependent plumbing entirely.

Another path I'm weighing is using convex-test to execute the real action handlers in a mocked environment with a fake identity, which still exercises the genuine rate limiting, entitlement checks, provider selection, and persistence logic—likely the strongest option since it runs authentic code against a fake DB while still hitting real LLM providers if configured.

Picking a provider does need a linked Not Organic DID seeded into the test database, and token issuance needs the signing env that evalConfiguration already sets up, so I should check how existing `.test.ts` files in convex/ already handle this.

What the user actually wants is for evals to run through the application's real harness—prompts, tools, parsing, Convex actions—driven via MCP, meaning the AI features themselves (persona feedback, room convening, rubric grading, extraction, research) need to be exposed as MCP tools.

They also want a CLI for the app so the same operations are scriptable and runnable in tests, with results logged to Arize for experiments, datasets, and traces. Since `@twyne/tools` already has a `twyne` CLI and `twyne-mcp` for data operations, the natural move is extending the integration API with AI operations like `room.convene`, `persona.run`, `rubric.review`, `judge.draft`, `research.extract`, and `interview.turn`, authenticated by PAT, then wiring those into both the CLI and MCP server so the eval harness can spawn `twyne-mcp` over stdio and call these tools directly—though I need to think about whether hosted AI access via PAT is actually acceptable here.

The complication is identity: these AI actions resolve the PAT to an owner `tokenIdentifier`, but the provider-picking logic calls `ctx.auth.getUserIdentity()` deep inside the 3340-line agents.ts, tying DID resolution to subject/tokenIdentifier directly rather than an explicit owner parameter — refactoring that properly would be substantial. An alternative is using Convex's local dev backend with `npx convex run` and its `--identity` flag, which lets me impersonate a user identity directly when invoking functions, potentially sidestepping the refactor entirely.

Running this requires a dev or local deployment plus an admin key, which for CI would mean pulling in the local backend binary — heavier than ideal for a test harness. I think the better path is a layered design: build an in-process harness module that reuses the real production code (prompt builders, tools, parsers from agentPrompts.ts/agentTools.ts) so tests exercise the same logic without needing a full deployment.

There seem to be two production paths — hosted via Convex's runLlm, and client-side BYOK via src/utils/ai-client.ts — and I need to check whether runLlm is pure enough to call directly or if its dependency on ActionCtx for streaming/usage makes that awkward. I'm leaning toward two transport adapters: a "local" one that runs the harness in-process with either a mock model for fast contract tests or a real gateway for evals, and a "remote" one that hits a deployed Twyne through the integration API to exercise the full hosted stack including auth and rate limiting.

I'm also thinking through surface area: new CLI commands (either added to the existing `twyne` CLI or a dedicated eval CLI), new MCP tools exposed via `twyne-mcp` so the eval runner can act as an MCP client against either transport, and uploading datasets/experiments to Arize via the `ax` CLI or SDK.

Twyne's default is autonomous, fluid action: editors read, research runs, reviews complete, and results arrive without the writer having to press a button. === twyne-browser-verification.md
---
name: twyne-browser-verification
description: "How to check twyne editor UI in a real browser here — headless Playwright env fix, free port, IndexedDB folio seeding, known flaky test pair"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
  originSessionId: 2a13dcae-f7b6-4086-b45c-4b7202355290
  modified: 2026-10-17T20:59:29.806Z
---

Recipe that worked on 2026-10-17 for verifying editor UI changes without the Convex backend:

- **Port:** 5173 may belong to another project (interleave-app). Start twyne with `TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 bun run dev.frontend`.
- **Headless Playwright:** importing `node_modules/playwright/index.mjs` from a scratch script works, but Chromium fails to launch (GLIBC error from a nix alsa-lib) unless run as `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH node script.mjs`.
- **Skip onboarding:** a fresh profile redirects /editor/ to /dossier/create/. Instead, seed like `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()`: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, visit a routed blank page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")` in page context, then call saveFoliosToIdb / saveFolioContentToIdb / saveActiveFolioIdToIdb (+ `signin-toast-dismissed` meta, `twyne:editor:view:v1` with zenMode false).
- **T3 preview tool:** its viewport can be zoomed or scaled (innerWidth ≠ the requested size), and evaluate/snapshot time out on heavy pages. Prefer the headless script for measurements.
- **Known flaky pair (pre-existing at HEAD bfa07af1):** `struggle-tracker.test.ts` and `quick-review.test.ts` fail together in one bun run (shared System One budget state). Each passes alone. Don't blame new changes for it.
- **Running e2e:** with the dev server on 5174, `env -u LD_LIBRARY_PATH TWYNE_DEV_PORT=5174 npx playwright test <file>` works.
  - Screenshot suites (instruments, instrument-dock, instrument-room, living-desk) must run under `--config playwright.visual.config.ts`. It starts its own server on 5187 and compares against the committed `e2e/visual-baselines/`. The default config writes stray `e2e/*-snapshots/` folders; delete them afterwards.
  - About 38 default-config e2e tests already failed at HEAD bfa07af1 (checked on 2026-10-17 against a clean worktree). The causes:
    - The Pagination extension was unregistered in 0cb77885, so `__twynePagination` never appears. This breaks all of pagination and formatting, and most of drag-selection.
    - The "Go to page" combobox needs the Typst proof, which never typesets here. This breaks editor-declutter.
    - Tests expect a visible `.twyne-toolbar`, Bold, or read-aloud control, but zen is now the default and those sit in the collapsed Compositor. This breaks __responsive, select-all and read-aloud.
    - Tests expect a "File ▾" button and other masthead and drawer flows that have since changed. This breaks import and dossier-persistence.
  - Before blaming a change, run the same files against `git worktree add --detach /tmp/twyne-base HEAD` on port 5175 and diff the failing test names. The BYOK and drop-caret tests flake.
- **Qwik gotcha:** a component inside a closed `<details>` never runs its `useVisibleTask$` (it has no box). Mount it only while the disclosure is open.

=== typst-compiler-constraints.md
---
name: typst-compiler-constraints
description: "Twyne's bundled Typst compiler is 0.14.x via typst.ts 0.7.0, with no package registry wired, so Universe packages requiring 0.15 or network fetch cannot be used as-is"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 45b242ab-0f38-465a-8599-1fa7f9343d32
  modified: 2026-10-19T01:29:29.128Z
---

As of 2026-10-18, `@myriaddreamin/typst.ts` 0.7.0 ships a WASM compiler whose version strings are Typst 0.14.0/0.14.1 (checked by grepping the wasm). The worker in `src/utils/typst/compiler.worker.ts` only bundles fonts and `addSource`/`mapShadow`; no `withPackageRegistry` is configured, so `#import "@preview/..."` fails offline. The native `title` element exists in 0.14 and is usable.

**Why:** Several desirable Universe packages (codly 2.0, touying 0.8, min-book, cheq) now require Typst 0.15; others (zebraw, cetz 0.5, fletcher 0.5.8, marginalia, droplet, verseatile, stagehand) run on 0.14 or earlier.

**How to apply:** Before proposing a Typst package for Twyne, check its `compiler` field in `https://packages.typst.org/preview/index.json`, and plan either to vendor the package through `mapShadow` or to add a package registry to the worker. See [[twyne-genre-kits-research]].

---
name: typst-compiler-constraints
description: "Twyne's bundled Typst compiler is 0.14.x via typst.ts 0.7.0, with no package registry wired, so Universe packages requiring 0.15 or network fetch cannot be used as-is"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 45b242ab-0f38-465a-8599-1fa7f9343d32
  modified: 2026-10-19T01:29:29.128Z
---

As of 2026-10-18, `@myriaddreamin/typst.ts` 0.7.0 ships a WASM compiler whose version strings are Typst 0.14.0/0.14.1 (checked by grepping the wasm). The worker in `src/utils/typst/compiler.worker.ts` only bundles fonts and `addSource`/`mapShadow`; no `withPackageRegistry` is configured, so `#import "@preview/..."` fails offline. The native `title` element exists in 0.14 and is usable.

**Why:** Several desirable Universe packages (codly 2.0, touying 0.8, min-book, cheq) now require Typst 0.15; others (zebraw, cetz 0.5, fletcher 0.5.8, marginalia, droplet, verseatile, stagehand) run on 0.14 or earlier.

**How to apply:** Before proposing a Typst package for Twyne, check its `compiler` field in `https://packages.typst.org/preview/index.json`, and plan either to vendor the package through `mapShadow` or to add a package registry to the worker. See [[twyne-genre-kits-research]].

content.thinking:
I'm noting that the server harness in convex/agents.ts handles an adaptive hosted LLM path with tools and telemetry sent to Arize via OpenInference, plus usage tracking. Now I'm thinking through the best architecture for building evals, since the user wants proper model evaluation rather than just application tests, and wants to continue leveraging Arize for this.

They want the evals to exercise the actual application harness—prompts, tool loop, orchestration—through an MCP server exposing those features as callable tools, plus a CLI for the app that's runnable in tests. The core design question becomes where the harness actually executes when invoked this way: a remote path through Convex hosted actions would use the real production code and existing Arize tracing, but requires network access during test runs.

I'm weighing that against running the harness locally in-process via Bun, importing the same modules the app uses with a swappable model provider (hosted eval client, OpenAI-compatible endpoint, or a deterministic fixture for tests). This local approach is cheap, reproducible, and test-friendly, but sacrifices some fidelity to production since parts of the real call path live in Convex node-runtime files.

So I'm considering a third option: a hybrid where the harness logic is factored into a pure, context-free module that both the Convex action and the local runner can share.

This is the more correct engineering approach since evals would measure the actual production code, but it means refactoring the 3340-line agents.ts that's already mid-change on this branch — risky but likely worth it long-term. I want to check how much of the harness logic is already context-free, starting with `runAdaptiveHostedLlm` and the adaptive review loop in `runAdaptiveEditorialDraft`, since that path is shared with the client already.

content.thinking:
I see the server harness is built from context-free shared pieces: prompt builders for system/user prompts, a tool builder that generates quote tools from draft text and research, and an adaptive editorial draft runner that handles operation, reasoning limits, generation, and review.

The context-dependent parts are provider selection, usage capture, research calls, System One access via ctx.runAction, stream mutations, and PostHog logging. A local harness could reuse the shared pieces while swapping in injected adapters -- a language model, optional research, an optional System One caller, a local usage ledger, and OTel telemetry routed to Arize -- without needing to refactor agents.ts, though I want to think about the drift risk if the Convex action adds new steps the local harness doesn't mirror.

The ideal would be extracting the generate/review composition into a shared `runEditorialNote(deps, req)` function used by both Convex and the CLI, though that means refactoring agents.ts, which already has uncommitted changes. Thinking about what the user actually wants -- running evals through the app's harness "as best it can via the mcp" and having a CLI so evals are runnable in tests -- I'm sketching the deliverables: a Twyne harness CLI with commands to run model-backed app operations locally against a chosen provider, something like a `twyne harness room` command taking a draft and brief as input.

I'm extending this to cover more harness commands (judge, rewrite, interview, extract), supporting an offline fixture-replay mode for tests. Then I'm outlining how to expose these as MCP tools in the twyne-mcp server so an eval runner or any agent can drive the harness that way, and sketching an eval runner that reads a dataset, spawns the MCP server, calls tools per case, scores outputs with deterministic and LLM-judge evaluators, and logs results to Arize as an experiment.

For traces, I'm planning to export OTel spans to a dedicated Arize project so each eval run carries full tracing, and testing this via bun test running the CLI/MCP in fixture mode for deterministic, network-free verification plus a smoke eval using the replay model. I'm also weighing whether the harness should eventually support a remote backend against a deployed Twyne instance, leaning toward designing the interface to allow a `--backend local|remote` switch later while implementing local-only for now.

Reconsidering the local-vs-remote question, I realize the "application harness" really means the same production code modules — prompts, tools, adaptive loop, parsers — minus the Convex plumbing, which fits "as best it can" well. Remote evals aren't feasible right now anyway, since the app's autonomous editors are triggered client-side in the browser rather than server-side, so a folio created purely via API wouldn't receive automatic feedback without an open browser session — confirming local is the right path, though I still need to figure out which harness pieces can actually run in Bun outside the browser.

I'm now tracing through the shared modules to see what's pure logic versus what's tightly coupled to Convex — the agent prompts and tools, the adaptive draft and editorial note review utilities, the writing lenses system, the rubric judges and their parsing, research target extraction, interview prompts, the Clairic extraction work, the dossier check, room synthesis, and the instrument task runner — mapping out dependencies across all of these to see what's portable.

I'm realizing the existing evals replay production prompts but each one re-implements the call-and-parse logic separately, which risks drift from the real actions. The cleanest fix would be centralizing everything into a single harness where both the Convex actions and the CLI call the same shared operation functions, though that means a real refactor of agents.ts and I need to weigh whether other concurrent work might be touching that file.

Given agents.ts has roughly fifteen actions, extracting all of them is too large for one pass, so I'm leaning toward a phased approach: start with a harness kernel for the most important model features built from shared pieces, plus a parity test confirming the harness produces identical prompts and tool sets to the real Convex action for matching inputs.

Rather than that, I could just extract the persona note composition (mapping the core adaptive hosted LLM call to the editorial note function) and the judge functions, which likely just build prompts, call generateText, parse JSON, and clamp results. Base directory for this skill: /home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne/.claude/skills/arize-experiment

# Arize Experiment Skill

> **`SPACE`** — All `--space` flags and the `ARIZE_SPACE` env var accept a space **name** (e.g., `my-workspace`) or a base64 space **ID** (e.g., `U3BhY2U6...`). Find yours with `ax spaces list`.

## Concepts

- **Experiment** = a named evaluation run against a specific dataset version, containing one run per example
- **Experiment Run** = the result of processing one dataset example -- includes the model output, optional evaluations, and optional metadata
- **Dataset** = a versioned collection of examples; every experiment is tied to a dataset and a specific dataset version
- **Evaluation** = a named metric attached to a run (e.g., `correctness`, `relevance`), with optional label, score, and explanation

The typical flow: export a dataset → process each example → collect outputs and evaluations → create an experiment with the runs.

## Prerequisites

Proceed directly with the task — run the `ax` command you need. Do NOT check versions, env vars, or profiles upfront.

If an `ax` command fails, troubleshoot based on the error:
- `command not found` or version error → see references/ax-setup.md
- `401 Unauthorized` / missing API key → run `ax profiles show` to inspect the current profile. If the profile is missing or the API key is wrong, follow references/ax-profiles.md to create/update it. If the user doesn't have their key, direct them to https://app.arize.com/admin > API Keys
- Space unknown → run `ax spaces list` to pick by name, or ask the user
- Project unclear → ask the user, or run `ax projects list -o json --limit 100` and present as selectable options
- **Security:** Never read `.env` files or search the filesystem for credentials. Use `ax profiles` for Arize credentials and `ax ai-integrations` for LLM provider keys. If credentials are not available through these channels, ask the user.
- **CRITICAL — Never fabricate outputs:** When running an experiment, you MUST call the real model API specified by the user for every dataset example. Never fabricate, simulate, or hardcode model outputs, latencies, or evaluation scores. If you cannot call the API (missing SDK, missing credentials, network error), stop and tell the user what is needed before proceeding.

## List Experiments: `ax experiments list`

Browse experiments, optionally filtered by dataset. Output goes to stdout.

```bash
ax experiments list
ax experiments list --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --limit 20   # DATASET_NAME: name or ID (name preferred)
ax experiments list --cursor CURSOR_TOKEN
ax experiments list -o json
```

### Flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `--dataset` | string | none | Filter by dataset |
| `--name, -n` | string | none | Substring filter on experiment name |
| `--limit, -l` | int | 15 | Max results (1-100) |
| `--cursor` | string | none | Pagination cursor from previous response |
| `-o, --output` | string | table | Output format: table, json, csv, parquet, or file path |

## Get Experiment: `ax experiments get`

Quick metadata lookup -- returns experiment name, linked dataset/version, and timestamps.

```bash
ax experiments get NAME_OR_ID
ax experiments get NAME_OR_ID -o json
ax experiments get NAME_OR_ID --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE   # required when using experiment name instead of ID
```

### Flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `NAME_OR_ID` | string | required | Experiment name or ID (positional) |
| `--dataset` | string | none | Dataset name or ID (required if using experiment name instead of ID) |
| `--space` | string | none | Space name or ID (required if using dataset name instead of ID) |
| `-o, --output` | string | table | Output format |

### Response fields

| Field | Type | Description |
|-------|------|-------------|
| `id` | string | Experiment ID |
| `name` | string | Experiment name |
| `dataset_id` | string | Linked dataset ID |
| `dataset_version_id` | string | Specific dataset version used |
| `experiment_traces_project_id` | string | Project where experiment traces are stored |
| `created_at` | datetime | When the experiment was created |
| `updated_at` | datetime | Last modification time |

## Export Experiment: `ax experiments export`

Download all runs to a file. By default uses the REST API; pass `--all` to use Arrow Flight for bulk transfer.

```bash
# EXPERIMENT_NAME, DATASET_NAME: name or ID (name preferred)
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE
# -> experiment_abc123_20260305_141500/runs.json

ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --all
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --output-dir ./results
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout | jq '.[0]'
```

### Flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `NAME_OR_ID` | string | required | Experiment name or ID (positional) |
| `--dataset` | string | none | Dataset name or ID (required if using experiment name instead of ID) |
| `--space` | string | none | Space name or ID (required if using dataset name instead of ID) |
| `--all` | bool | false | Use Arrow Flight for bulk export (see below) |
| `--output-dir` | string | `.` | Output directory |
| `--stdout` | bool | false | Print JSON to stdout instead of file |

### REST vs Flight (`--all`)

- **REST** (default): Lower friction -- no Arrow/Flight dependency, standard HTTPS ports, works through any corporate proxy or firewall. Limited to 500 runs per page.
- **Flight** (`--all`): Required for experiments with more than 500 runs. Uses gRPC+TLS on a separate host/port (`flight.arize.com:443`) which some corporate networks may block.

**Agent auto-escalation rule:** If a REST export returns exactly 500 runs, the result is likely truncated. Re-run with `--all` to get the full dataset.

Output is a JSON array of run objects:

```json
[
  {
    "id": "run_001",
    "example_id": "ex_001",
    "output": "The answer is 4.",
    "evaluations": {
      "correctness": { "label": "correct", "score": 1.0 },
      "relevance": { "score": 0.95, "explanation": "Directly answers the question" }
    },
    "metadata": { "model": "gpt-4o", "latency_ms": 1234 }
  }
]
```

## Create Experiment: `ax experiments create`

Create a new experiment with runs from a data file.

```bash
ax experiments create --name "gpt-4o-baseline" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --file runs.json
ax experiments create --name "claude-test" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --file runs.csv
```

### Flags

| Flag | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| `--name, -n` | string | yes | Experiment name |
| `--dataset` | string | yes | Dataset to run the experiment against |
| `--space, -s` | string | no | Space name or ID (required if using dataset name instead of ID) |
| `--file, -f` | path | yes | Data file with runs: CSV, JSON, JSONL, or Parquet |
| `-o, --output` | string | no | Output format |

### Passing data via stdin

Use `--file -` to pipe data directly — no temp file needed:

```bash
echo '[{"example_id": "ex_001", "output": "Paris"}]' | ax experiments create --name "my-experiment" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --file -

# Or with a heredoc
ax experiments create --name "my-experiment" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --file - << 'EOF'
[{"example_id": "ex_001", "output": "Paris"}]
EOF
```

### Required columns in the runs file

| Column | Type | Required | Description |
|--------|------|----------|-------------|
| `example_id` | string | yes | ID of the dataset example this run corresponds to |
| `output` | string | yes | The model/system output for this example |

Additional columns are passed through as `additionalProperties` on the run.

## Delete Experiment: `ax experiments delete`

```bash
ax experiments delete NAME_OR_ID
ax experiments delete NAME_OR_ID --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE   # required when using experiment name instead of ID
ax experiments delete NAME_OR_ID --force   # skip confirmation prompt
```

### Flags

| Flag | Type | Default | Description |
|------|------|---------|-------------|
| `NAME_OR_ID` | string | required | Experiment name or ID (positional) |
| `--dataset` | string | none | Dataset name or ID (required if using experiment name instead of ID) |
| `--space` | string | none | Space name or ID (required if using dataset name instead of ID) |
| `--force, -f` | bool | false | Skip confirmation prompt |

## Annotate Runs: `ax experiments annotate-runs`

Write annotations onto experiment runs in bulk from a file. Upsert semantics — existing annotations with the same key are updated, new ones are created. Up to 1000 annotations per request.

```bash
ax experiments annotate-runs NAME_OR_ID --file annotations.json --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE
ax experiments annotate-runs NAME_OR_ID --file annotations.csv --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE
```

### Flags

| Flag | Type | Required | Description |
|------|------|----------|-------------|
| `NAME_OR_ID` | string | yes | Experiment name or ID (positional) |
| `--file, -f` | path | yes | Annotation file: JSON, JSONL, CSV, or Parquet (use `-` for stdin) |
| `--dataset` | string | yes | Dataset name or ID (required when using experiment name instead of ID) |
| `--space` | string | no | Space name or ID |

## Experiment Run Schema

Each run corresponds to one dataset example:

```json
{
  "example_id": "required -- links to dataset example",
  "output": "required -- the model/system output for this example",
  "evaluations": {
    "metric_name": {
      "label": "optional string label (e.g., 'correct', 'incorrect')",
      "score": "optional numeric score (e.g., 0.95)",
      "explanation": "optional freeform text"
    }
  },
  "metadata": {
    "model": "gpt-4o",
    "temperature": 0.7,
    "latency_ms": 1234
  }
}
```

### Evaluation fields

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `label` | string | no | Categorical classification (e.g., `correct`, `incorrect`, `partial`) |
| `score` | number | no | Numeric quality score (e.g., 0.0 - 1.0) |
| `explanation` | string | no | Freeform reasoning for the evaluation |

At least one of `label`, `score`, or `explanation` should be present per evaluation.

## Workflows

### Run an experiment against a dataset

1. Find or create a dataset:
   ```bash
   ax datasets list --space SPACE
   ax datasets export DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout | jq 'length'
   ```
2. Export the dataset examples:
   ```bash
   ax datasets export DATASET_NAME --space SPACE
   ```
3. Call the real model API for each example and collect outputs. Use `ax datasets export --stdout` to pipe examples directly into an inference script:

   ```bash
   ax datasets export DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout | python3 infer.py > runs.json
   ```

   Write `infer.py` to read examples from stdin, call the target model, and write runs JSON to stdout. The script below is a template — first inspect the exported dataset JSON to find the correct input field name, then uncomment the provider block the user wants:

   ```python
   import json, sys, time

   examples = json.load(sys.stdin)
   runs = []

   for ex in examples:
       # Inspect the exported JSON to find the right field (e.g. "input", "question", "prompt")
       user_input = ex.get("input") or ex.get("question") or ex.get("prompt") or str(ex)

       start = time.time()

       # === CALL THE REAL MODEL API HERE — never fabricate or simulate ===
       # Uncomment and adapt the provider block the user requested:
       #
       # OpenAI (pip install openai  — uses OPENAI_API_KEY env var):
       #   from openai import OpenAI
       #   resp = OpenAI().chat.completions.create(
       #       model="gpt-4o",
       #       messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
       #   )
       #   output_text = resp.choices[0].message.content
       #
       # Anthropic (pip install anthropic  — uses ANTHROPIC_API_KEY env var):
       #   import anthropic
       #   resp = anthropic.Anthropic().messages.create(
       #       model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=1024,
       #       messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
       #   )
       #   output_text = resp.content[0].text
       #
       # Google Gemini (pip install google-genai  — uses GOOGLE_API_KEY env var):
       #   from google import genai
       #   resp = genai.Client().models.generate_content(
       #       model="gemini-2.5-pro", contents=user_input
       #   )
       #   output_text = resp.text
       #
       # Custom / OpenAI-compatible proxy (pip install openai — uses CUSTOM_BASE_URL + CUSTOM_API_KEY env vars):
       # Use this for Azure OpenAI, NVIDIA NIM, local Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint,
       # including a test integration proxy. Matches the `custom` provider in `ax ai-integrations create`.
       #   import os
       #   from openai import OpenAI
       #   resp = OpenAI(
       #       base_url=os.environ["CUSTOM_BASE_URL"],          # e.g. https://my-proxy.example.com/v1
       #       api_key=os.environ.get("CUSTOM_API_KEY", "none"),
       #   ).chat.completions.create(
       #       model=os.environ.get("CUSTOM_MODEL", "default"),
       #       messages=[{"role": "user", "content": user_input}]
       #   )
       #   output_text = resp.choices[0].message.content

       latency_ms = round((time.time() - start) * 1000)
       runs.append({
           "example_id": ex["id"],
           "output": output_text,
           "metadata": {"model": "MODEL_NAME", "latency_ms": latency_ms}
       })
       print(f"  {ex['id']}: {latency_ms}ms", file=sys.stderr)

   json.dump(runs, sys.stdout, indent=2)
   ```

   **Before running:** install the provider SDK (`pip install openai` / `anthropic` / `google-genai`) and ensure the API key is set as an environment variable in your shell. If you cannot access the API, stop and tell the user what is needed.

4. Verify the runs file:
   ```bash
   python3 -c "import json; runs=json.load(open('runs.json')); print(f'{len(runs)} runs'); print(json.dumps(runs[0], indent=2))"
   ```
   Each run must have `example_id` and `output`. Optional fields: `evaluations`, `metadata`.
5. Create the experiment:
   ```bash
   ax experiments create --name "gpt-4o-baseline" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --file runs.json
   ```
6. Verify: `ax experiments get "gpt-4o-baseline" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE`

### Compare two experiments

1. Export both experiments:
   ```bash
   ax experiments export "experiment-a" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout > a.json
   ax experiments export "experiment-b" --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout > b.json
   ```
2. Compare evaluation scores by `example_id`:
   ```bash
   # Average correctness score for experiment A
   jq '[.[] | .evaluations.correctness.score] | add / length' a.json

   # Same for experiment B
   jq '[.[] | .evaluations.correctness.score] | add / length' b.json
   ```
3. Find examples where results differ:
   ```bash
   jq -s '.[0] as $a | .[1][] | . as $run |
     {
       example_id: $run.example_id,
       b_score: $run.evaluations.correctness.score,
       a_score: ($a[] | select(.example_id == $run.example_id) | .evaluations.correctness.score)
     }' a.json b.json
   ```
4. Score distribution per evaluator (pass/fail/partial counts):
   ```bash
   # Count by label for experiment A
   jq '[.[] | .evaluations.correctness.label] | group_by(.) | map({label: .[0], count: length})' a.json
   ```
5. Find regressions (examples that passed in A but fail in B):
   ```bash
   jq -s '
     [.[0][] | select(.evaluations.correctness.label == "correct")] as $passed_a |
     [.[1][] | select(.evaluations.correctness.label != "correct") |
       select(.example_id as $id | $passed_a | any(.example_id == $id))
     ]
   ' a.json b.json
   ```

**Statistical significance note:** Score comparisons are most reliable with ≥ 30 examples per evaluator. With fewer examples, treat the delta as directional only — a 5% difference on n=10 may be noise. Report sample size alongside scores: `jq 'length' a.json`.

### Download experiment results for analysis

1. `ax experiments list --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE` -- find experiments
2. `ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE` -- download to file
3. Parse: `jq '.[] | {example_id, score: .evaluations.correctness.score}' experiment_*/runs.json`

### Pipe export to other tools

```bash
# Count runs
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout | jq 'length'

# Extract all outputs
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout | jq '.[].output'

# Get runs with low scores
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout | jq '[.[] | select(.evaluations.correctness.score < 0.5)]'

# Convert to CSV
ax experiments export EXPERIMENT_NAME --dataset DATASET_NAME --space SPACE --stdout | jq -r '.[] | [.example_id, .output, .evaluations.correctness.score] | @csv'
```

## Related Skills

- **arize-dataset**: Create or export the dataset this experiment runs against → use `arize-dataset` first
- **arize-prompts**: Store and version the prompt template in Prompt Hub (`ax prompts`) before or after experiments
- **arize-prompt-optimization**: Use experiment results to improve prompts → next step is `arize-prompt-optimization`
- **arize-trace**: Inspect individual span traces for failing experiment runs → use `arize-trace`
- **arize-link**: Generate clickable UI links to traces from experiment runs → use `arize-link`

## Troubleshooting

| Problem | Solution |
|---------|----------|
| `ax: command not found` | See references/ax-setup.md |
| `401 Unauthorized` | API key is wrong, expired, or doesn't have access to this space. Fix the profile using references/ax-profiles.md. |
| `No profile found` | No profile is configured. See references/ax-profiles.md to create one. |
| `Experiment not found` | Verify experiment name with `ax experiments list --space SPACE` |
| `Invalid runs file` | Each run must have `example_id` and `output` fields |
| `example_id mismatch` | Ensure `example_id` values match IDs from the dataset (export dataset to verify) |
| `No runs found` | Export returned empty -- verify experiment has runs via `ax experiments get` |
| `Dataset not found` | The linked dataset may have been deleted; check with `ax datasets list` |

## Save Credentials for Future Use

See references/ax-profiles.md § Save Credentials for Future Use.

I'm identifying which harness modules are pure and portable versus which depend on Convex context—provider selection, usage/PostHog capture, research, and System One calls all need ctx, suggesting I should think through two possible layering approaches for running evals, starting with an in-process option.

For option A, I'm sketching an offline app harness that composes the same pure pieces the server uses but with an injected model (AI SDK, mock, or eval client), letting the CLI run locally and be testable without Convex. But I realize this risks duplicating the Convex action's composition logic, so the better path is refactoring both into a shared "editorial engine" parameterized by ports—model provider, System One caller, research source, telemetry—so Convex and the CLI/evals just plug in different port implementations.

I'm weighing the risk though: agents.ts is 3340 lines with other threads possibly touching it, though checking the uncommitted diff shows it's only 22 lines and other active work (Typst, share button) likely avoids that file, so the refactor seems feasible.

Now I'm considering a second layer — a deployed harness exposed through the integration API and MCP, adding operations like room.convene as MCP tools and CLI commands so evals can drive a real dev/prod deployment end-to-end, testing auth, rate limits, routing, persistence, and the whole pipeline, which would require a PAT and a linked DID for hosted AI access.

Since the user explicitly wants evals to use the application harness via MCP, and wants a CLI runnable in tests, I'm sketching a design where the MCP server gains AI tools — convening the room of editors on a folio, asking a single persona for feedback, suggesting rewrites, and grading drafts against a rubric with judges and a chief reviewer.

I'm extending this out: a CLI with matching commands (room convene, editor ask, grade, eval run) supporting JSON output, and two interchangeable backends — a remote deployment hitting the integration API with PAT auth, and a local in-process harness mode with an injected mock model provider for tests and offline evals without needing a live deployment.

But packaging is tricky — `@twyne/tools` needs to stay a clean publishable package without app dependencies, while the local harness needs access to app internals like prompts and utilities, so it should probably live inside the app repo itself with the CLI using some transport abstraction to switch between backends.

Actually, `convex-test` is already a dependency and could run Convex functions in-process against a mocked database with a real identity — essentially giving the application harness for free in tests. The open question is whether "use node" actions and external fetch calls work properly inside that mocked environment, and how environment variables get handled there.

Since `pickProvider` falls back to `pickLegacyProvider()` using env API keys when Not Organic isn't enabled, we could configure a provider via env vars pointing at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint and exercise it through convex-test. I'm also realizing convex-test supports HTTP actions via `t.fetch`, so the integration route could be tested that way too.

This leads me to a nice architectural insight: since TwyneClient already accepts a custom `fetch`, in tests we can create a user and PAT via an internal mutation, then wire the client's fetch straight to `t.fetch`, routing requests through the in-process backend. The MCP server built on that client could then be connected via an in-memory transport pair, giving us a fully in-process, testable end-to-end setup.

But I'm now second-guessing whether convex-test actually handles "use node" actions properly, since it loads modules via `import.meta.glob`, which may not be available under Bun test. I should check how the existing convex tests here are configured to see if this pattern already works.

There's also the "live" mode to consider: pointing the same CLI/MCP setup at a real dev/prod deployment with a PAT. content.thinking:
Convex tests run under vitest with edge-runtime, which supports `import.meta.glob`, but `bun test` skips those. I'm wondering whether the "use node" actions file, which pulls in OpenTelemetry's node SDK, will even work properly under edge-runtime given that dependency.

I should just test this directly rather than reason about it further — maybe spin up a scratch vitest file inside the convex directory to see if convex-test can actually invoke `api.agents.judgeDraft` in-process, then delete it afterward. But before going deeper into this experiment, I want to zoom out and settle the overall architecture first, since the user wants me to use Astra and Fable, and that should shape how I delegate this work.

Thinking through what matters most to the user: better evals for model behavior than the current tests, continued use of Arize for datasets/experiments/evaluators/traces, evals driven through the application harness via MCP, and a CLI for the app that's runnable in tests. I'm sketching a "Twyne eval harness v2" architecture — adding integration API operations and an MCP/CLI surface covering things like persona feedback and rewrites on drafts, rubric grading with judges and a chief critic, dossier checks, research target extraction, and interview turns, plus possibly room-level analysis operations.

Each of these would map to an internal action variant taking an explicit userId derived from the PAT, with existing public actions refactored to share handler logic under an explicit identity rather than relying on ctx.auth. I'm weighing whether these AI operations should persist results into the folio or stay stateless — stateless "run and return" seems simplest for evals, while persistence could still be handled by the client sync layer, with the integration's feedback.get reading stored notes. For MCP-driven external agents, returning feedback directly feels most natural, with an optional persist flag to also save results into the folio so the writer sees them in-app.

Also, the PAT itself is a personal access token with full account access, so these AI operations need to run against hosted credits and respect rate limits via consumeRateLimit. For a local in-process test backend, I'm thinking about using convex-test to boot the app, create a user and PAT, and route a TwyneClient's fetch through t.fetch, with the MCP server connected via InMemoryTransport — the tricky part is getting pickProvider to use a mock language model inside convex-test rather than a real provider, since it normally builds providers from env keys.

I'm considering a module-level test override hook like setProviderOverrideForTests, mirroring the existing setClientUsageRecorderForTests pattern, and reasoning through whether convex-test's module loading via import.meta.glob shares the same module instance as a direct import in vitest (it should, since the module cache is shared).

Then I reconsider the user's actual request — they likely want a CLI for the application itself that can be driven by tests and evals, rather than just an in-process test harness, so I need to figure out what backend that CLI should target.

I'm weighing pointing the CLI at a real deployment via PAT versus spinning up a local Convex backend binary for full-fidelity testing with real node actions, though that path requires downloading the local backend, deploying functions to it, and managing env vars without clobbering the existing dev deployment config.

Given the risk, I'm leaning toward a tiered approach: Tier 1 uses convex-test's in-process backend with an in-memory MCP transport and a scripted mock model to verify the full wiring deterministically in vitest, while Tier 2 reuses that same in-process backend but swaps in real models for offline evals.

Tier 3 would then point the actual CLI/MCP at a deployed environment with a real PAT, exercising the full production path including routing and live responses.

I'm now wondering whether convex-test can actually run node actions with real network calls and the AI SDK, so I want to write a quick probe test checking whether agents.ts's imports behave correctly under vitest's node environment. I should also look into whether the `ai` SDK's mock models could help here.

On the eval-scorer side, I'm noting the current evals rely on LLM judges through Not Organic, which need credentials like NOTORGANIC_*, TWYNE_EVAL_DID, and TWYNE_EVAL_MAX_COST_MICROUSD that aren't present in skate -- only other provider keys like NeuralWatt, Thinking Machines, Typesafe, and PriorLabs are available there.

The Not Organic secrets likely live server-side in the Convex deployment environment rather than skate, so I'd need to check there, and for both the judge model and the model under test I still need to figure out which provider to actually use.

I'm thinking I should make the provider configurable—supporting Not Organic, OpenAI-compatible, Anthropic, or a mock—so an OpenAI-compatible option could point to NeuralWatt's endpoint if I can confirm its base URL from the earlier experiment metadata in Arize rather than guessing. I also want to use Astra Fable to split this into lanes, starting with the Convex backend integration API work as the first lane.

Since Fable (claude-fable-5-1) looks like Anthropic's most capable model in the family listing, I should assign it the hardest, most delicate part — the identity-explicit internal actions, provider override hook for tests, and the convex-test harness factory within the large Convex file. The second lane, handled by Astra (gpt-6-astra), covers the CLI and MCP tool surface in packages/twyne-tools plus the eval runner with scorers, Arize upload, and OTLP tracing — though that's a lot, so I'm considering splitting it further so Astra focuses on CLI/MCP and the eval runner while Fable stays on the backend.

I'll handle integration, review, dataset curation, Arize setup, and docs myself. Since the CLI/MCP work depends on the backend's API contract, I need to define operation names and request/response shapes upfront in the delegation briefs so both lanes can proceed in parallel, and before finalizing I want to quickly verify that convex-test works with node actions in agents.ts and check the ai/test mocks.

I'm checking how the HTTP integration route dispatches operations and resolves user identity, since internal actions lack `ctx.auth`, meaning the agent handler functions need to be passed an explicit `ownerId` instead.

I need to trace how `pickProvider` derives the subject from the identity's tokenIdentifier, since PAT-authenticated calls supply `userId` as the full tokenIdentifier string and I need to extract just the subject portion for `productSubject`. The core issue is that PATs aren't JWTs, so identity doesn't propagate automatically through `ctx.runAction` the way it does for HTTP-authenticated requests. The real fix is refactoring these AI actions into shared handler functions that accept identity explicitly as an argument, with the public action deriving it from `ctx.auth` and an internal variant deriving it from args for the PAT-based integration route -- and propagating that explicit identity through every nested helper that currently calls `ctx.auth.getUserIdentity()` directly.

One alternative worth considering: have the CLI exchange its PAT for a short-lived Convex-compatible auth JWT via an exchange endpoint, then use that JWT directly with `ConvexHttpClient.setAuth()` to call the public actions as if authenticated normally, sidestepping the need to thread identity through manually.

But minting full sessions from PATs would expand their power to everything—billing, account deletion—since Better Auth's token-issuing API requires an actual session. That's too broad a security surface compared to a narrower, explicit allowlist of integration operations, which seems safer.

For the in-process test tier, I realize I don't need a PAT at all—I can use `t.withIdentity(...)` to call public actions directly, bypassing the HTTP layer entirely. That raises the idea of having the MCP server's in-process client call the same public actions directly with an identity, rather than going through the integration API's HTTP endpoint, while still exercising the same code paths the browser uses.

But for live deployments the HTTP integration API is required regardless, so I still need to build AI operations support there to cover Tier 3. I'm also checking what existing eval datasets already exist to build on.

I'm thinking through the architecture for the eval runner: a suites directory where each suite defines its dataset, how to execute a case through MCP tool calls, and its scorers; a CLI runner that executes cases concurrently, collects outputs and scores, writes results to disk, and uploads everything to Arize as datasets and experiments; and separate target implementations, starting with an in-process target that boots a convex-test app.

I'm now working out how convex-test resolves module paths since it needs a `modules` map keyed by file path, and without vite's `import.meta.glob` I'll need to build that map manually via a file walk and dynamic imports, matching the key format convex-test expects relative to the convex directory.

Running this under Bun or tsx instead of vitest should work fine since Bun is largely Node-compatible, and the earlier probe already succeeded under node. I'm also noting that the live target spawns the twyne-mcp server over stdio using the deployed app's API URL and access token, while the in-process target wires things differently.

For the in-process path, I create a PAT through the integrations API with an identity, build a TwyneClient pointing at a test URL with fetch routed through convex-test, then spin up the MCP server and client over an in-memory linked transport so the suite can call tools directly. This means the eval genuinely traverses MCP → HTTP route → internal actions → the real harness → the model, using an actual provider config rather than a mock -- though I need to check whether Not Organic mode requires a linked DID for this in-process setup to work correctly.

Given the legacy provider selection order checks RIVET_ENDPOINT before API keys, setting env vars in-process feels hacky, so I'm considering adding a cleaner eval-friendly provider override, though module-level state could get tricky with how convex-test loads modules.

I'm also thinking about System One and extraction calls to external services — since internal actions without auth get a null identity, persona research gets disabled and degrades to a bare reserve. These datasets are pretty small, and a stronger eval suite really needs more and better cases — curating good ones with known flaws and ground-truth labels could itself be a meaningful lane of work. With that in mind, I'm starting to map out the lanes, beginning with Fable.

For Lane A, I'm focused on the backend harness surface in Convex: threading explicit caller identity through the hosted AI paths so the same handler logic works for both public actions and PAT-authenticated internal actions, adding a new integration module for operations like note-editing, rubric judging/grading, interview turns, and dossier checks, wiring these into the HTTP integration switch with folio resolution, and building a test seam for overriding model selection during in-process evals. I'm also planning convex-test coverage using a mock language model to verify identity scoping, response shapes, PAT auth, and error handling.

Now I'm thinking about Lane B — the tools surface across the CLI and MCP package. This involves adding typed client methods for each new operation, exposing them as new MCP tools (expanding the tool count from 10 to 17, which means updating the README and tool name list plus tests), and adding corresponding CLI subcommands for editors, rubric, interview, and dossier operations with JSON output, file/stdin input options, and proper exit codes.

For Lane C, which is mine, I'm scoping out the eval runner: an in-process target that boots a convex-test app outside vitest, sets up a writer identity and PAT, wires a TwyneClient through that fetch, and runs an MCP server/client pair over an in-memory transport, plus a model provider override seam for testing. I also need a live target that runs the MCP CLI over stdio against a real deployment, and I'm sketching out eval suites starting with editor persona notes testing groundedness, helpfulness, and anchoring.

I'm also planning the remaining suites — rubric discrimination pairs for judge calibration, integrity/evidence checks for bullshit detection, rewrite meaning-preservation, and interview protocol tests — along with scorers split into deterministic checks (anchor validity, quote validity, JSON contract, score range) and LLM judges mirrored against Arize evaluators, plus pairwise discrimination scoring. For Arize integration I'm working out dataset upserts per suite, experiment creation with run metadata and OTLP spans, and I need to make sure the in-process target sets the Arize env vars before importing convex modules since arizeTracing reads env at module load time.

Given the scope, I think the right split is to delegate the eval-suite surfaces to the helper agents while I own the eval runner and Arize wiring myself, since that piece integrates both lanes — I can build it against the existing 10 tools now and wire in new tools once the other lanes land. I also need to think through the shared checkout situation given other active threads and uncommitted state before proceeding.

Looking at file ownership, lanes A and B touch disjoint areas (convex/* vs packages/twyne-tools/*) while I'm in evals/app/*, package.json, and docs — the main conflict risk is the generated Convex API types and package.json scripts. I'm leaning toward a shared checkout rather than worktrees since the branch already has uncommitted work this builds on, so I'll tell the delegates to avoid committing, avoid running full suites, stay within their lanes, and not revert anyone else's changes.

I also need to make sure delegates don't commit or stash, and don't run checkout/restore commands, since the repo has uncommitted work on this branch I shouldn't disturb. I'll let Fable figure out the exact codegen invocation, falling back to hand-editing api.d.ts if needed since it's a simple generated pattern. Now I need to think about which model provider to use for in-process evals—whether to go through the Not Organic gateway with eval credentials or another option.

The most faithful approach is wrapping the Not Organic eval route with eval DID to mirror production routing, so the same aliases resolve to the same upstream models as prod. Alternatively, I could use an OpenAI-compatible endpoint like NeuralWatt, OpenRouter, or a local llama.cpp instance via a configurable base URL.

The override seam should take a feature and alias and return a provider config, letting evals map aliases like balanced or reasoning to specific models or pass through to Not Organic's own alias resolution — this keeps judges and persona generation consistent with how production actually routes requests.

For judging, I'll need a separate `--judge` config to specify the LLM-as-judge model, reusing the existing evals chat completion client for Not Organic or OpenAI-compatible providers. Credentials-wise, the NeuralWatt key lives in skate, but I should check an earlier Arize experiment's metadata to confirm the right API base URL before wiring it up — though that's not strictly necessary right now. A small smoke run of maybe 10 calls against a cheap model is trivial in cost and fits what they're asking for, so I'll do that and leave full runs to them — especially since they've already used NeuralWatt for twyne evals before. For tracing, I need to remember the Arize skill's rule: never read .env files directly, always use ax profiles or skate-stored values for ARIZE_API_KEY and ARIZE_SPACE_ID, exporting them from skate into the environment, and use the ax CLI for dataset/experiment uploads with the already-configured profile.

So instead I'll compute evaluations locally and attach them to experiment runs, since the schema supports an evaluations field. For tracing, arizeTracing.ts registers an OTel provider that exports OpenInference spans whenever ARIZE_API_KEY and ARIZE_SPACE_ID are set before module load, so for eval runs I should set a separate ARIZE_PROJECT_NAME like twyne-evals to keep them distinct from production traces, along with ARIZE_CAPTURE_CONTENT since the eval data is synthetic.

I think consolidating is the answer — folding related AI operations into fewer, broader tools rather than one tool per operation. I'm trying to consolidate the editor-related tools into a smaller set to stay within the 15-tool cap—considering whether a single "convene room" tool could handle both single-editor and multi-editor note-taking, though mixing those semantics complicates how evals map to tools. I keep sketching different five-tool AI groupings to fit the overall count.

Dossier check has an eval-able contract too, so I'll settle on five AI tools for MCP: convene_room, ask_editor, suggest_rewrite, grade_draft, and interview_turn, with editor persona info embedded in tool descriptions. The CLI keeps all seven operations including editors list and dossier check, and I need to update the README plus the test expecting a fixed tool count — though I'm second-guessing whether changing that "exactly 10" assertion is safe.

Looking at the test name again, "requested names" implies this was a prior ask for exactly those 10, and the ≤15 cap suggests 15 is the true hard limit, so expanding to 15 fits within it — I'll update the test's expected list and title and note this in my summary. Dependency resolution looks fine since the twyne-tools package has its own node_modules with the SDK, marked, and zod, which take precedence over the root's versions. As a more realistic alternative, I'm considering having the eval runner spawn the built MCP binary over stdio pointed at the local app's HTTP port, so I'll support both an in-memory default and a stdio option that requires the app to listen on a real port. For the eval suites, I'm planning to reuse the existing dataset and rubric JSONL files for the room/editor suite where they fit.

# App harness: AI operations over the integration API, CLI and MCP

Twyne's model-backed features (the room of editors, rewrites, the rubric, the
dossier check and the dossier interview) are reachable from outside the
browser through the same authenticated boundary the folio tools already use:
`POST /api/integrations/v1` with a personal access token. The `twyne` CLI and
the `twyne-mcp` server in `packages/twyne-tools` expose them, and the app evals
in `evals/app/` drive them through MCP, so an eval exercises the production
path rather than a replay of its prompts.

```
eval runner ──MCP──▶ twyne-mcp tools ──TwyneClient──▶ /api/integrations/v1
                                                       │  (PAT → owner)
                                                       ▼
                                 internal actions in convex/ (same code the
                                 browser's api.agents.* actions run)
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
                                 hosted provider: Not Organic, or the legacy
                                 OpenAI-compatible route (RIVET_ENDPOINT)
```

## Operations

Every request is `{ "operation": "<name>", ...fields }` and every success is
`{ "ok": true, "data": ... }`, exactly like the folio operations. Failures are
`{ "ok": false, "error": "..." }` with the same public-error filtering.

Shared field types:

- `draftText: string` — the manuscript as plain text.
- `folioId: string` — alternative to `draftText`. The server loads the
  owner's folio, converts its HTML to plain text, and uses the folio's brief
  when `brief` is not supplied. Supplying neither is a 400.
- `brief: ProjectBrief | null` — the dossier (`convex/agents.ts`
  `projectBriefValidator`). Optional everywhere except `dossier.check`.
- `responseLocale: "en" | "fr" | "es" | "zh" | "hi" | "ja"` — optional.
- `writerProfile` — optional, `writerProfileValidator` shape.
- `personaId` — one of the built-in editors in `src/utils/personas.ts`:
  `devil`, `angel`, `scholar`, `editor`, `reader`.

`EditorNote`:

```ts
{
  personaId: string;
  personaName: string;
  text: string;
  type: "critique" | "suggestion" | "encouragement" | "perspective";
  provider: string;          // "local" means the hosted model was not used
  anchor?: string;           // verbatim passage pinned by quote_passage
  anchors?: string[];
  extractions?: unknown[];
  traceId?: string;
}
```

| operation         | fields                                                                                                                                 | `data`                              |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `editors.list`    | —                                                                                                                                      | `Array<{ id, name, role, description, focus }>` |
| `room.convene`    | `draftText`\|`folioId`, `brief?`, `personaIds?` (default: all five), `writerProfile?`, `responseLocale?`, `newMaterial?`, `trajectory?` | `{ notes: EditorNote[] }`           |
| `editor.ask`      | `personaId`, `draftText`\|`folioId`, `brief?`, `instruction?` (`feedback`\|`elaborate`\|`riff`\|`rewrite-suggestion`), `userMessage?`, `priorMessages?`, `anchor?`, `writerProfile?`, `responseLocale?` | `{ note: EditorNote }` |
| `rewrite.suggest` | `personaId`, `draftText`\|`folioId`, `original`, `level` (`sentence`\|`paragraph`), `brief?`, `writerProfile?`, `responseLocale?`         | `{ replacement, rationale, provider }` |
| `rubric.grade`    | `draftText`\|`folioId`, `brief?`, `criteria?: Array<{ label, description }>`, `responseLocale?`                                            | `RubricGrade` (below)               |
| `dossier.check`   | `brief`, `draftText`\|`folioId`, `responseLocale?`                                                                                      | `{ observations, provider }`        |
| `interview.turn`  | `messages: Array<{ author: "writer"\|"interviewer", text }>`, `mode` (`first-run`\|`refine`), `currentBrief?`, `startingMaterial?`, `responseLocale?` | `InterviewTurnResult` (as `runInterviewTurn` returns) |

`RubricGrade` mirrors what the rubric panel computes on its hosted path:

```ts
{
  grade: string;            // letter grade from combineJudgesAndStatic
  combined: number;
  judgeMean: number;
  minJudge: number;
  staticTotal: number;
  staticFeedback: string[];
  judges: Array<{ personaId: string; score: number; rationale: string; provider: string }>;
  sufficiency: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  evidence: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  integrity: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  targetFit: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  custom: Array<{ label: string; score: number; rationale: string; provider: string }>;
  review: { text: string; provider: string } | null;
}
```

Model-backed operations apply the same per-owner rate limits as the browser
actions. Results are returned, not written to the folio.

## Running the app locally for tests and evals

`evals/app/local-app.ts` loads every module in `convex/` into one process with
`convex-test`, seeds a writer and an access token, and serves the real HTTP
router. Hosted calls go wherever the environment points them:

- `--model mock` starts a scripted OpenAI-compatible stub and sets
  `RIVET_ENDPOINT` to it, so the legacy hosted route answers from fixtures.
- `--model openai-compatible` uses `TWYNE_APP_MODEL_BASE_URL`,
  `TWYNE_APP_MODEL_API_KEY` and `TWYNE_APP_MODEL` through the same route.
- `--model notorganic` keeps the app's Not Organic routing and links the
  seeded writer to `TWYNE_EVAL_DID`.

```sh
bun evals/app/local-app.ts --model mock --port 8788
# prints TWYNE_API_URL and TWYNE_ACCESS_TOKEN for the CLI and twyne-mcp
```

the `twyne-mcp` server in `packages/twyne-tools` expose them, and the app evals

path rather than a replay of its prompts.

```
                                 browser's api.agents.* actions run)
                                                       │
                                                       ▼
                                 hosted provider: Not Organic, or the legacy
                                 OpenAI-compatible route (RIVET_ENDPOINT)
```

## Operations

Every request is `{ "operation": "<name>", ...fields }` and every success is
`{ "ok": true, "data": ... }`, exactly like the folio operations. Failures are
`{ "ok": false, "error": "..." }` with the same public-error filtering.

Shared field types:

- `draftText: string` — the manuscript as plain text.
- `folioId: string` — alternative to `draftText`. The server loads the
  owner's folio, converts its HTML to plain text, and uses the folio's brief
  when `brief` is not supplied. Supplying neither is a 400.
- `brief: ProjectBrief | null` — the dossier (`convex/agents.ts`
  `projectBriefValidator`). Optional everywhere except `dossier.check`.
- `responseLocale: "en" | "fr" | "es" | "zh" | "hi" | "ja"` — optional.
- `writerProfile` — optional, `writerProfileValidator` shape.
- `personaId` — one of the built-in editors in `src/utils/personas.ts`:
  `devil`, `angel`, `scholar`, `editor`, `reader`.

`EditorNote`:

```ts
{
  personaId: string;
  personaName: string;
  text: string;
  type: "critique" | "suggestion" | "encouragement" | "perspective";
  provider: string;          // "local" means the hosted model was not used
  anchor?: string;           // verbatim passage pinned by quote_passage
  anchors?: string[];
  extractions?: unknown[];
  traceId?: string;
}
```

| operation         | fields                                                                                                                                 | `data`                              |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `editors.list`    | —                                                                                                                                      | `Array<{ id, name, role, description, focus }>` |
| `room.convene`    | `draftText`\|`folioId`, `brief?`, `personaIds?` (default: all five), `writerProfile?`, `responseLocale?`, `newMaterial?`, `trajectory?` | `{ notes: EditorNote[] }`           |

| `rewrite.suggest` | `personaId`, `draftText`\|`folioId`, `original`, `level` (`sentence`\|`paragraph`), `brief?`, `writerProfile?`, `responseLocale?`         | `{ replacement, rationale, provider }` |
| `rubric.grade`    | `draftText`\|`folioId`, `brief?`, `criteria?: Array<{ label, description }>`, `responseLocale?`                                            | `RubricGrade` (below)               |
| `dossier.check`   | `brief`, `draftText`\|`folioId`, `responseLocale?`                                                                                      | `{ observations, provider }`        |

```ts

  grade: string;            // letter grade from combineJudgesAndStatic
  combined: number;
  judgeMean: number;
  minJudge: number;
  staticTotal: number;
  staticFeedback: string[];
  judges: Array<{ personaId: string; score: number; rationale: string; provider: string }>;
  sufficiency: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  evidence: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  integrity: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  targetFit: { score: number; rationale: string; provider: string };
  custom: Array<{ label: string; score: number; rationale: string; provider: string }>;
  review: { text: string; provider: string } | null;
}
```

Model-backed operations apply the same per-owner rate limits as the browser
actions. Results are returned, not written to the folio.

`evals/app/local-app.ts` loads every module in `convex/` into one process with

router. Hosted calls go wherever the environment points them:

- `--model mock` starts a scripted OpenAI-compatible stub and sets
  `RIVET_ENDPOINT` to it, so the legacy hosted route answers from fixtures.
- `--model openai-compatible` uses `TWYNE_APP_MODEL_BASE_URL`,
  `TWYNE_APP_MODEL_API_KEY` and `TWYNE_APP_MODEL` through the same route.
- `--model notorganic` keeps the app's Not Organic routing and links the
  seeded writer to `TWYNE_EVAL_DID`.

```sh
bun evals/app/local-app.ts --model mock --port 8788
# prints TWYNE_API_URL and TWYNE_ACCESS_TOKEN for the CLI and twyne-mcp
```
