{"case_id": "rewrite-story-stairs-sentence", "personaId": "editor", "level": "sentence", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "The Keeper's Daughter", "format": "opening of a short story", "audience": "readers of literary short fiction", "goal": "put the reader inside Nell's head at the moment she chooses silence, and make the choice feel earned", "tone": "close third person, slow, exact", "constraints": "under 900 words; stay in Nell's point of view", "successSignal": "a reader believes a nine-year-old would make this choice and is frightened for her"}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "Nell had been told to count the seconds between the flashes, and she counted them the way she had been taught, with a "Mississippi" after each number, though she had never seen the Mississippi and privately doubted it existed. Four. The light swung round and went out over the water and came back. Four again. Her father said that was how a sailor knew which light he was looking at, because every lighthouse in the world had its own time, like a heartbeat, and a sailor who knew the heartbeats could tell where he was in the dark from forty miles out.

She was nine. It was the first night he had let her sit up in the lamp room, and she had promised not to touch anything, and she had kept the promise for almost an hour.

The lamp itself was behind her, inside its glass, turning on its bath of mercury with a sound like a very slow clock. Her father was below, winding the weight. She could hear the chain going up through the tower in jerks, and his breath between the jerks, and under that the sea, which was the sound she had stopped hearing years ago and had to remember to listen for, the way you have to remember to notice that you are breathing.

Out on the water there was a ship. She saw its lights first, red and green, and then the dark shape between them, and she counted it as she counted everything: a ship, one Mississippi, still there. It was closer than ships usually came. Her father had said the rocks ran out a mile from the point and that was why the light was here, to tell the ships about the rocks, and this ship did not seem to have been told.

She should have called down. She knew that. She thought of the chain going up and her father's breath, and she thought that if she called down he would come up and look and say it was nothing, a fishing boat, and then he would not let her sit up again, and so she watched the ship instead, and counted, and the light went round.

Thomas, winding the weight, had been thinking about the girl's mother, which he did most nights at about this hour, when the work was mechanical and the mind went where it wanted. He did not hear the ship. He did not hear anything but the chain. He was thinking that the girl had her mother's way of looking at a thing as if it owed her an explanation, and that it would get her into trouble, and that he would not be there for all of it.

The ship's green light went out. Nell waited for it to come back and it did not, and she understood, in the slow way that a child understands things that are too large, that the ship had turned, and that the side of it she could see now was the side with no light on it, and that it was turning toward the rocks.

She went to the top of the stairs. She did not call. She stood at the top of the stairs with her hand on the rail, which was cold, and which she was not supposed to touch, and she looked down into the dark of the tower and listened to the chain, and she thought very clearly, and in words, for the first time in her life: if I say nothing, this is mine.

The sea was very calm that night, calmer than it had been for a month, and the sky was clear and there was no wind at all, and the stars were out over the water in their thousands, and the whole of the bay lay under them as still as a plate, and the ship went on turning.

Below her, the chain stopped. Her father's breath stopped with it, and then there was his voice, coming up the tower, saying her name, not loudly, the way he said it when he already knew something was wrong. She did not answer. The light went round. Four Mississippi. They will be built for dentists, or freight brokers, or the people who run car washes, and they will be worth more than the horizontal tools they replace. This is not a prediction about niches. It is a prediction about where the margin went.

For twenty years the standard advice was to build the general tool. Make the spreadsheet, the CRM, the project tracker, and let every industry adapt it. The logic was that a big market beats a small one, and that a tool used by every company would be worth more than a tool used by one kind. The logic was right as long as the hard part was building the software. It is no longer the hard part.

What is hard now is knowing the customer. A freight broker does not want a CRM. She wants to know which of her forty carriers will actually show up on Thursday, and she wants the software to already know that a load from Harrowfield to the port needs a tarp and a driver with a hazmat endorsement. The general tool can be configured to do this, by someone, eventually. The vertical tool does it on the first day, because the people who built it used to be freight brokers.

Look at the companies that have actually compounded. Toast started as a restaurant point-of-sale and became the restaurant's bank. ServiceTitan sells to plumbers and is worth more than most of the horizontal tools its customers used to patch together. Procore owns construction. In each case the company began by solving one workflow completely and then found that the customer, having trusted it with the workflow, would trust it with the payments, the payroll, the lending and the insurance.

Our analysis of the 212 vertical software companies that raised a Series A between 2015 and 2020 found that they reached 10 million dollars in annual recurring revenue a median of fourteen months faster than horizontal companies in the same cohort, and that their gross retention at year three averaged 94 percent against 81.

This is why the vertical company wins. It can charge for the workflow and then take a percentage of the money that flows through it. The horizontal tool charges a subscription and watches the money go past.

The objection is obvious: the market is small. There are only so many dentists. But the number that matters is not the count of customers; it is the share of each customer's revenue you can touch. A dental practice turns over around a million dollars a year. Touch three percent of that across ten thousand practices and you have a business larger than most horizontal tools will ever be, selling to people who will never leave because leaving means re-entering their patients' records by hand.

The counterargument that matters more is the one people do not raise: that the vertical company's moat is also its ceiling. The freight-broker tool is wonderful at freight brokerage and useless for anything else, and when the industry contracts, as freight does every few years, the software contracts with it. The horizontal tool is dull but it is diversified.

I think this is a fair point and that it does not change the conclusion.

It is also worth saying, because people do say it, and it needs to be addressed, that there is a question about whether the examples that get cited in essays like this one are the examples that happened to work, and whether there is a longer list, somewhere, of vertical companies that did not, and that nobody writes essays about.

The practical advice, then. If you are starting a company, pick an industry you have worked in, not one you have read about. Find the workflow its people hate most and do that one thing until it is boring. Then, and only then, go after the money that moves through it. The companies that did this are the ones that compounded. The companies that built a general tool and hoped a vertical would adopt it are, mostly, the ones that got acquired for less than they raised.

The general tool was the right answer when software was scarce. Software is no longer scarce. Knowledge of the customer is, and the vertical company is simply the form that knowledge takes when it decides to charge rent.", "original": "I think this is a fair point and that it does not change the conclusion.", "problem": "The essay's strongest objection is conceded and dismissed in one sentence with no reason given; the rewrite must actually answer the ceiling-versus-moat objection or admit the limit.", "mustPreserve": ["conclusion"]}

{"case_id": "rewrite-memo-objection-paragraph", "personaId": "devil", "level": "paragraph", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Residential vacancy in the central wards", "format": "policy briefing memo", "audience": "the seven members of the Housing and Planning Committee", "goal": "get the committee to adopt a residential vacancy levy at its next meeting", "tone": "neutral, evidence-led, recommendation up front", "constraints": "under 900 words; the recommendation must appear in the first two paragraphs; every figure must be sourced", "successSignal": "a committee member can state the recommendation, the rate and the expected revenue after one read"}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "To: Housing and Planning Committee
From: Policy Analysis Unit
Re: Residential vacancy in the central wards

Over the past three years the committee has received a growing volume of correspondence about homes in the central wards that appear to be unoccupied for most of the year. This memo sets out what we know about the scale of the problem, reviews the approaches other cities have taken, and offers an assessment of the options available to the council.

Background. The central wards contain roughly 18,400 dwellings. Utility data obtained under the information-sharing agreement with Ellery Water indicates that 1,460 of these, or 7.9 percent, used less than ten percent of median household water consumption in each of the last four quarters, which is the threshold the agreement defines as "likely unoccupied." This figure has risen from 5.1 percent in the first year of the agreement. The increase is concentrated in buildings completed after 2019 and in the two wards closest to the harbour.

Unoccupied housing in these numbers has costs. Street-level retail depends on resident footfall, and the Harbour Ward business association reports vacancy among ground-floor units of 22 percent. School rolls in the central wards have fallen while enrolment elsewhere in the city has risen. Units held empty are units not available to the 3,100 households currently on the council's housing register.

Other cities. Vancouver introduced an Empty Homes Tax in 2017 at one percent of assessed value, later raised to three percent; the city reports that the number of vacant properties fell by more than half over four years, though some of that decline reflects owners reclassifying properties rather than letting them. Melbourne's vacant residential land tax applies at one percent and has been criticised as too low to change behaviour. Verenport, whose housing market most closely resembles ours, adopted a two percent levy in 2021 and recorded a 38 percent reduction in likely-unoccupied units within two years, with 61 percent of the revenue directed to its affordable housing fund.

We should note that the evidence base is small, that cities differ in enforcement capacity, and that the Vancouver data in particular has been contested by the development industry.

Options. The committee has, broadly, three choices. It can take no action and continue monitoring. It can pursue voluntary measures, such as a registry of long-term vacant units and a matching service connecting owners with the housing register. Or it can introduce a levy on dwellings unoccupied for more than six months in a year, with exemptions for probate, renovation, and medical absence.

Our recommendation is that the committee adopt the third option, a levy of two percent of assessed value, phased in over two years, with the first year at one percent. We estimate first-year revenue at 11 to 14 million dollars before behavioural response, declining as owners let or sell. We recommend that the revenue be ring-fenced for the housing fund.

The main argument against a levy is that it is a tax on ownership rather than on harm, and that owners have legitimate reasons for leaving a property empty. The exemptions address this. The remaining cases, owners who hold property empty as a store of value, are exactly the cases the levy is meant to reach, and it is difficult to see why the council should protect them.

A second concern is enforcement. The water-consumption method produces an indicator, not a determination, and some owners will dispute it. We propose a self-declaration model, as in Vancouver, with the water data used to target audits rather than to assess liability directly. Audit capacity of two full-time staff should be sufficient in the first year.

It should also be said, and it is worth the committee bearing this in mind as it considers the matter, that this is a question on which public opinion in the city has, over the period in question, become considerably more engaged than it was previously, and that the committee's handling of it will be watched with some interest.

The levy will not solve the housing shortage. It will not build a single home. What it will do is return several hundred existing homes to use within two years, fund the construction of others, and signal that the council regards a dwelling as something to live in. These are modest goals. They are also the only ones available to the committee this year.", "original": "The main argument against a levy is that it is a tax on ownership rather than on harm, and that owners have legitimate reasons for leaving a property empty. {"case_id": "rewrite-salt-dates-sentence", "personaId": "scholar", "level": "sentence", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Salt Roads", "format": "travel essay for the Journeys & Returns collection", "audience": "readers of literary travel writing who have never heard of the Salters' Way", "goal": "walk the reader along the road and leave them with one idea about what a road remembers", "tone": "observant, dry, lyrical only when earned", "constraints": "under 900 words; every distance and date should be checkable", "successSignal": "a reader can describe the road's three surfaces and say what Doug thinks of the question"}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "The salt road starts where the sea used to be. At Marrow Haven the pans are a car park now, flat and white in the wrong way, and the only sign that anyone ever boiled brine here is a plaque the council put up in 1987, which gets the century wrong. I read it twice, decided not to care, and walked inland.

For four hundred years, from the time the monks at Keld Priory first leased the pans in 1312 until the railway killed the trade in the 1840s, packhorses carried salt along this track: thirty-eight miles from the coast to the market at Keld, two days with a load, three in rain. The route is older than the salt. Flint turns up along it, and a Roman milestone sits in the churchyard at Scarrow, which is where I slept the first night, in a barn that had been a barn when the milestone was new.

I had come to walk the road because I wanted to know what a road remembers. That is the kind of sentence you write before you set out. By the second morning, with my boots not yet dry and the moor opening ahead like a grey sea with the water taken out, I had stopped wanting to know anything and simply wanted the next stile.

The salters walked in trains of twenty horses, each horse carrying two hundredweight in panniers, which comes to roughly two tonnes of salt per train. A train left Marrow Haven every weekday in the season. At that rate the road carried more salt in a year than the whole county eats now, and it did it on a track you could lose in bracken.

The surface tells you where you are. Near the coast it is sand over clay, and the horses' feet have worn it into a hollow way three metres deep, so that you walk between walls of root and earth with the sky a strip overhead. Up on the moor it is peat and stone, and the road is a line of slightly greener grass, marked at intervals by cairns that someone still maintains. Coming down into the valley of the Keld it becomes a lane with a tarmac spine and grass shoulders, and then a road, and then a street with a butcher on it.

The road forgot the sea entirely somewhere around the twelfth mile. I kept looking back for it and there was only moor. The salt had come from there, and the horses had come from there, and the track had been made by nothing but their wanting to get away from it, and yet nothing about it now said sea. It said sheep. It said wind. It said, mostly, nothing, which is what moors say.

At Scarrow I met a man named Doug who has walked the road, by his count, over nine hundred times. He is seventy-one and does it in a day, there and back, when the weather is right, which he said it rarely is. He told me the cairns on the moor are not old at all; his father built the biggest one in 1952 after two walkers died in fog, and the one before that fell down in a storm nobody remembers. I asked him what the road remembered. He looked at me the way you would look at someone who had asked a sheep what it thought of the view.

The thing about a salt road, I want to say, and I say it knowing that it is the sort of thing a person says who has been walking for two days on not much sleep and has started to find significance in stiles, is that salt is the one cargo that does not leave a trace, because it dissolves, so that the whole road is a record of something that is no longer there.

Keld, when I got there, was having a market. Not a salt market; it sells cheese now, and candles, and a kind of fudge. I bought the fudge. I sat on the steps of the cross where the salt had been weighed and ate it and watched the town not remember anything at all, and it occurred to me that the road did not need to remember, because it was still there, which is what roads do instead.", "original": "For four hundred years, from the time the monks at Keld Priory first leased the pans in 1312 until the railway killed the trade in the 1840s, packhorses carried salt along this track: thirty-eight miles from the coast to the market at Keld, two days with a load, three in rain.", "problem": "1312 to the 1840s is more than five hundred years, not four, and the lease is asserted without a source; the rewrite should fix the span and signal where the date comes from or how firm it is.", "mustPreserve": ["Keld Priory", "1312", "1840s", "thirty-eight miles"]}

The brain, which produces waste faster than almost any other tissue, has no such vessels inside it. Neurons make junk, the junk goes somewhere, and nobody could say where.

In 2012 a group at the University of Rochester watched the answer happen in mice. I made the eval DID and ran 22 real cases on Not Organic, but it can't do the full run yet. It only holds the $2.50 welcome credit Not Organic grants automatically, and the room and rubric suites need about $10 of headroom. That's because each call reserves its full ceiling up front ($0.50 `balanced`, $2.00 `reasoning`), even though each actually costs cents. A full room on the welcome credit failed for that reason.

**The DID:** `did:plc:h7t2qykaxwf6s7iez6pmhs45` (`twyne-evals.pds.notorganic.info`), created on your PDS. The DID and password are in skate (`twyne-eval-did`, `twyne-evals-pds-password`), and the account email is your Gmail with `+twyne-evals`. I signed it in to id.notorganic.info once so Not Organic knows it.

**Your step:** Admin → Accounts → `twyne-evals.pds.notorganic.info` → Direct grant **$47.50**, product scope **Twyne**. With the welcome credit that's exactly $50. Nothing else can draw on this wallet, so your cap is enforced by Not Organic itself. I couldn't do the grant myself: no checkout on this machine is linked to production Not Organic, and I didn't want to pull your admin secret out of Railway.

**Gateway problem found:** with the new DID, every paid call came back as a bare 500. The cause is the "session version" Twyne sends with each request. Twyne defaults to 1, a DID that has never had a Not Organic account record is at 0, and the gateway rejects the mismatch with an error it doesn't map. I added `TWYNE_EVAL_SESSION_VERSION`, which defaults to 1 so existing evals don't change, and set it to 0 for this DID. Separately, Not Organic should probably return a 401 there instead of an opaque 500; I didn't touch its code.

**Results so far** (interview, rewrite, dossier; 0 errors, every case answered by the hosted model):

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| Dossier check | Flagged 4/4 planted brief drifts. |

| Rewrite | Always changes the passage. Keeps 75% of must-keep facts: the op-ed rewrite dropped "this city", and the reader editor translated away the term "AQP4". 1 in 8 breaks the length rule. |

Some of those first numbers were my scorers' fault (0.44 and 0.70 before fixes). I fixed the scorers, corrected two corpus entries that weren't facts, and deleted the two Arize experiments uploaded with the wrong scores. content.thinking:
I'm looking at the real room results: every note stays grounded in its source and gets rated helpful, but plant coverage is weak—only about half the planted features get noticed, with factual errors, buried ledes, and audience gaps all showing up at meaningful rates, and longer drafts fare even worse on coverage.

The anchor_spread of 0.68 suggests editors tend to overlap on the same passages rather than spreading attention. This points to a key insight: the faithfulness/helpfulness judges are too lenient to catch what matters, while plant coverage is the metric that actually discriminates quality—but that metric is itself constrained by format, since each editor writes just one note per convening, capping coverage at five notes for five-to-six plants regardless of model skill. So I should flag that "50% coverage" partly reflects this one-note-per-editor design limit, not just model quality, though notes mentioning multiple plants via shared word runs complicates the counting.

I'm also noting token costs — roughly 11.4k input tokens per editor call across 50 calls — and that actual dollar cost will show up once the wallet reports in, alongside the rubric suite and monitor output. I want to compute the theoretical ceiling for plant coverage given the plants-to-notes ratio, since the observed 0.49 is well below the ~0.85 max, and factor in the expected_editor metric of 0.41 reflecting whether the right specialist editor caught each plant.

content.text:
The room suite is the most informative so far:

- **Mechanics are solid.** 50/50 notes were written by the hosted model, all 50 anchored to verbatim passages, and the five editors sound distinct (0.98).
- **The LLM judges barely discriminate.** Faithfulness is 1.00 and helpfulness 0.98. These are the same rubrics as your Arize evaluators, and they pass nearly everything.
- **Planted problems are where the signal is.** The room noticed about half of them (0.49). The weakest kinds were factual errors (2/6), buried ledes (1/4) and audience gaps (2/7). On the long drafts it falls to 13–25%. Even the problems the editors could see there were mostly missed (0.33).

Part of the coverage ceiling is by design: one convening produces one note per editor, so five notes chase five or six plants. I'll account for that in the final read. The rubric suite is running now.

I should pull up the log to see how the cases actually resolved.

The first rubric case failed completely with a 503 provider_unavailable error across all judges, which triggers the runner's stop guard after 3 consecutive failures. The problem is that the `stopped` flag is scoped globally at the runAppEvals level, so it would incorrectly skip the remaining suites too, even though those use a different judge model.

The cleanest path is to kill the current run, investigate whether the `reasoning` alias failure is consistent or transient, then restart the remaining suites separately so they're not wrongly blocked by an unrelated alias issue.

I should test directly: make one simple chat completion to the reasoning alias with no tools to confirm it errors, and verify balanced still works. I shouldn't patch the app to route around the broken alias — the real finding is that rubric grading is currently broken in production on Not Organic's reasoning alias, and that's what needs to be reported, especially since the room judges (faithfulness/helpfulness) succeeded earlier using the same default model.

The likely cause is that the persona system prompt instructs the model to call quote_passage before claims, but in the judge path that prompt is reused without actually providing the tool — so the model attempts a tool call with none available, triggering an upstream rejection. That points to an app bug where judgeDraft/judgeRoom reuse a tool-referencing system prompt without supplying the tools.

I should also decide whether to kill the background run now, since it's likely burning through failed rubric calls while reservations might not release promptly on failure.

Once this stop guard trips, it cascades across all suites, skipping every remaining case, and I worry the final upload step could then choke on empty experiment runs and abort entirely. Better to kill the run now before that happens.

The `reasoning` judges all errored on the first rubric case, and since repeated failures would trip my stop guard and tie up wallet funds via unused $2 reservations, I'm stopping the run here—results so far are already saved and in Arize.

The bug itself: rubric judges and rewrite suggestions use an editor prompt that instructs the model to call `quote_passage` before any claim, but those particular calls don't expose tools. This caused the model to emit a tool call that got rejected upstream, triggering retries, 502s, and fallback behavior across 5 call sites. I fixed it by appending a no-tools prompt block whenever tools are disabled, confirmed the default prompt path is untouched, and all 34 prompt tests pass -- the rubric suite went from failing to 8/8. I'm now realizing this same failure mode could be hitting production judges right now, since `judgeRoom` calls the system prompt builder without tools too, meaning real users may be silently falling back to canned heuristic responses.

The fix lives in the working tree but hasn't actually been deployed, and I need to make clear that production grades could currently be partly fabricated by the fallback. I also want to note that the related 500 errors seemed to accompany the 502 tool-rejection errors — likely retries causing idempotency replay failures — and both error types disappeared entirely after the fix. There's still a separate reliability issue where a chunk of rubric judge scores seem affected by a reasoning-mode model burning its whole output budget on reasoning before producing an answer.

Because there's no output ceiling set, the gateway falls back to the provider default, and the reasoning model exhausts it, leaving empty content — the app then silently substitutes a canned local score that looks like a real judgement. I see a few fix options: cap reasoning effort for judges, retry with a different alias when content is empty, or surface an "unjudged" state instead of faking a score. content.text:
The full run is done: 40 cases across all five suites, no errors, all uploaded to Arize. Getting there exposed a production bug, which I fixed.

**The bug:** the rubric judges and suggested rewrites use the editor prompt, which tells the model to call `quote_passage` before making any claim. Those calls offer no tools, so a model that obeys gets its response rejected ("model called a tool when tool_choice='none'"). The app then silently substitutes a canned score, or shows "AI service unavailable". It hits three server paths and the two equivalent bring-your-own-key paths in the browser, so it's likely degrading grades in production now. The fix is a `prompts/blocks/no-tools.md` block, added only to those five tool-less calls; every other prompt is unchanged. The rubric suite went from failing its first case to 8/8, and the 34 prompt tests pass. It isn't deployed.

**A second problem, not fixed:** 19% of rubric judgements still come from the canned local fallback. The `reasoning` model sometimes spends its entire output budget thinking (about 17k characters) and returns empty text. The writer then sees an editor's score that no model produced, e.g. "The argument moves, but the strongest counter-objection is still unstated." I'd retry an empty judgement once on `balanced` and mark it unjudged if that also fails, rather than inventing a score. Say if you want that.

**What the evals say about the model:**
- **The LLM judges can't tell good notes from bad.** Faithfulness scores 1.00 and helpfulness 0.98. These are the same rubrics as your Arize evaluators, so the real signal is in the planted-problem checks.
- **Room coverage is about half.** It caught 49% of planted problems, and only 19% on long chapters. Even the problems the editors could see in a long draft were mostly missed (0.33), so the 4,500-character clamp isn't the whole story; they mostly comment near the top. Weakest at factual errors, buried ledes and audience gaps.

import json, re
fold = lambda s: re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s.replace("“",'"').replace("”",'"').replace("‘","'").replace("’","'")).strip()
room = json.load(open("reports/app-evals/notorganic-full-20261023-room.json"))

    for n in c["raw"]["notes"]:
        if n.get("extractions"): ext += 1
        a = n.get("anchor")

        i = d.find(fold(a))
        if i < 0: continue
        rel = i / max(1, len(d)); anchors_n += 1
        buckets[min(4, int(rel*5))] += 1

For clamped long drafts, the visible portions are head and tail, and anchors landing in the tail reinforce this recency effect — I should fix my earlier claim and recommend instructing editors to scan the whole draft or restructuring prompts so instructions appear both before and after the draft.

Separately, I'm noting that research tools were never used in any of the fifty notes, which seems worth flagging.

On the evidence judge: remote-work-strong got a "3" score but it's actually a fallback to local heuristics because the hosted judge failed, not a genuine LLM evaluation — that's a reasoning-output bug, not an evidence problem. The sourdough case reveals a deeper flaw: the judge demands citations even for practical how-to content where specific mechanisms and diagnostic tests should count as evidence instead, penalizing the strong and weak twins equally regardless of actual claim quality — the judge needs to account for genre.

564-  // Mean across judges, with a hard penalty for any judge below 4.

566-    judges.length > 0
567-      ? judges.reduce((s, j) => s + j.score, 0) / judges.length
568-      : 5;
569-  const lowJudges = judges.filter((j) => j.score < 4).length;
570-  const lowPenalty = lowJudges * 0.4; // each low judge drags the mean

573-  // The harshest single judge, weighted heavily on its own — one persona
574-  // calling the draft broken shouldn't get diluted away by an average.

582-

content.thinking:
Interesting, the room position bias isn't at the top of the draft like I expected—anchors and plants both cluster in the last 40%. This makes sense given the clamp only preserves head and tail text, so editors naturally anchor in the tail for long drafts, meaning middle plants risk being missed.

I'm also checking whether research tools got used at all—extractions came back empty across all 50 notes, so the model never called extract, find_passages, or judge even though they should have been available on the Not Organic linked path. That tells me either the tools weren't actually offered or the model simply never leveraged them.

Looking at the evidence judge rationales, one case (rubric-remote-work-strong) is a local-fallback artifact from exhausted reasoning budget rather than a genuine judge failure, while another (sourdough-strong) seems like a defensible call—the judge is penalizing an explainer with specific claims but zero citations, which fits the evidence judge's mandate to check whether claims needing evidence are actually backed by it.

The real inconsistency is that the judge treats first-hand observation and worked numbers as valid evidence in some cases (slow-train scoring 7, grant-renewal scoring 8) but not others (sourdough getting only 3 for lacking citations), suggesting the prompt needs to better distinguish genre-appropriate evidence types from strict citation requirements. I also want to check the evidence_order metric, which came out at 0.88 due to one tied pair, pointing toward broader reliability concerns with this judge.

For actual fixes versus measurement issues: the room coverage problem (0.49 overall, dropping to 0.19 on long drafts) seems like a harness constraint — the 4,500-character clamp is only about 1,100 tokens, far too small for modern hosted models with much larger context windows, so raising that limit substantially (to something like 24k characters) would let the model actually see full drafts.

The cost math checks out: current token usage is around 11.4k tokens per note call, and expanding the clamp would add maybe 10k tokens per note across two calls, which seems acceptable. Since `buildUserPrompt` is shared across both browser and local paths, raising the clamp affects everyone equally — though I need to think about how this interacts with BYOK local models running with much smaller context windows like 8k.

A 24k-character draft could overflow an 8k-context local model once the system prompt is added in, so the clamp might need to vary by provider rather than being a single fixed value. I'm also noticing the find_passages tool exists exactly to let editors search beyond the clamped window in long manuscripts, so maybe the design intent is for research tools to compensate rather than widening the base clamp — I want to check whether notes are actually using multiple anchors from that tool.

I'm also realizing coverage is capped by design: since each editor submits just one focused note per convening, coverage can never exceed 5 notes against 6-8 planted issues (0.83 or 0.625 max). That means the eval shouldn't measure raw coverage but something like note precision — what fraction of submitted notes actually target a planted problem.

Given that, the 49% figure is roughly 59% of the achievable cap, which isn't as damning as it first looked. I should add an uncapped "note-on-plant" metric that measures landing rate independent of the one-note-per-editor constraint.

On the product side, the real fix is raising the context clamp so long chapters aren't trimmed to 4.5k characters for hosted editors, since that's genuinely limiting coverage. I'm also noticing the room distinguishes background passes (which cover new material since last read) from explicit convenes (which clamp the whole draft) — so I need to figure out what the intended coverage behavior actually is for long manuscripts, especially given the per-persona anchors and windowed passage selection already in place.

Separately, for the rubric fallback issue, the fix is to retry once when the judgement comes back empty before falling back locally.

But I also need to think about how the panel combines scores -- currently local fallbacks get treated as normal judge scores in the mean. A better approach would be to exclude local fallback scores from the average when at least one hosted judge succeeded, rather than fabricating a number, though that's more of a product decision than a pure bug fix.

Tracing where the empty output actually comes from: the judge call goes through trackedGenerateText with a reasoning-tier model, and the text ends up empty after stripping reasoning tags, so parseJudgeOutput returns null and triggers the local fallback. It looks like the reasoning model is hitting a max output token ceiling mid-thought (finish reason "length" with empty content but ~17.9k chars of reasoning), suggesting the default output budget is too small for this reasoning alias.

Possible fixes: switch persona judges to a "balanced" alias since their output is just a score plus one sentence and doesn't need heavy reasoning effort, or retry with "balanced" specifically when the reasoning response comes back empty due to hitting the length limit, preserving reasoning quality when it does work. I should also check whether the gateway exposes a reasoning-effort parameter, since the AI SDK's OpenAI provider supports configuring that via provider options.

For the actual implementation, I'll retry once with the "balanced" alias when a judge returns a null/unparseable result, and for legacy providers that lack aliases, retry with the same model but a nudge prompt telling it to answer now without extended reasoning. If it still fails after retry, I need to figure out how to mark that judge as unjudged given the JudgeResult type expects a numeric score — maybe exclude it from aggregation entirely rather than forcing a score.

This touches several consumers of judge results though: rubric-panel.tsx (both hosted and client paths), rubric-room-grade.ts, and the combine logic. The issue is the panel currently displays local judge rationales as if the editor actually generated them, so fabricated text would need to be replaced with something like "this editor couldn't be reached" for unjudged cases — which means UI changes in a large file I'd rather not disturb if others are touching it.

Let me scope the fix more concretely: retry once when a judge's output is empty or unparseable on the balanced tier, for both the core judgers and the dimension judges; then in the combine step, exclude local-provider judges from the mean whenever at least one hosted judge responded, so a fallback never shifts the grade, while static features still count. Since both rubric-room-grade.ts and the panel's hosted path call combineJudgesAndStatic, fixing it there benefits both — though I still need to check how the client BYOK path handles judges coming from client providers.

Now I'm checking how the UI panel surfaces local judges — whether it already labels them as unreached or if I need to add that distinction so users know a fallback occurred rather than a real evaluation.

For the evidence judge inconsistency, I want to refine its prompt so it weighs evidence relative to genre and audience — a popular explainer shouldn't be penalized for lacking citations the way an academic piece would, but it should still be expected to show named sources, first-hand observation, concrete data, or clearly explained mechanisms appropriate to its form.

For the rewrite task dropping must-keep facts like AQP4, I'm tightening the instructions to say every name, number, and technical term the passage depends on must stay unless the term itself is the stated problem. I need to check the actual case definition — if the "jargon" problem means the term should be explained rather than deleted, then the rewrite removing AQP4 entirely is a clear violation, which matches what the judge already flagged.

Now looking at where the rewrite prompt actually lives, I see it's inline in both the server-side and client-side code (not in the prompts markdown files), so I'll need to add the fact-preservation instruction to both locations rather than a single shared file.

Shifting to the interview case, I'm checking a flagged "miss" where the model asked about a success signal that was genuinely never established in the conversation — comparing against the expected dossier fields to confirm whether this was actually a gap or a false flag.

Actually the model's question about success signal is justified by the prompt's own field list, since it explicitly names piece, reader, goal, tone, constraints, success signal, and advisors as required elements. So the case expectation may be wrong rather than the model's behavior — the fix should probably be on the scorer side, not by suppressing legitimate follow-up questions.

the terse-but-complete case to clarify that synthesis should happen once the four core fields are present, rather than second-guess the model's reasonable question. The scorer should treat asking about a genuinely missing field as a distinct "asked-missing-field" outcome rather than a flat miss, since the model isn't wrong to probe for it even if the case expected synthesis.

For the premature-synthesis-risk case, I'm now weighing whether inferring "workingTitle" from a vague mention of a wedding speech counts as legitimate dossier-building or an unsupported stretch, since no DOSSIER entry was actually recorded.

On the LLM judge saturation problem, I'm thinking the fix is to replace the binary grounded/generic and good/poor scoring with a more discriminating graded rubric, like a 1-5 scale.

Rather than just tweaking the existing judge templates, it's probably better to add new judged metrics: specificity (does the note make a claim that would be false for a different draft?), actionability (is there a concrete next step?), and accuracy (is the claim about the draft actually true?). I'm also considering a planted-feature alignment check — whether the note addresses a real planted weakness versus a trivial nit — since we already have deterministic plant coverage to compare against.

I'm thinking the right move is a single graded judge call returning specific/correct/actionable sub-scores on a 1-5 scale, normalized, while keeping the existing faithfulness/helpfulness checks for continuity since they're cheap signals even if saturated. The real issue might be that anchored notes quoting the draft make "grounded" too easy to satisfy under a binary rubric — a graded rubric should fix that. I still need to check git blame on the 4500 clamp for long drafts, and the hosted 0.81 rubric issue should already be resolved by the earlier fix.

Separately, the portal wallet showing $0.00 looks like a bug in the Not Organic portal repo, unrelated to this work — probably grants not being surfaced correctly. Going back through the user's list of issues, I want to map each one to a fix: the 19% canned fallback, judges failing to distinguish good from bad notes, room coverage gaps on long chapters, the evidence judge unfairly scoring strong drafts low, rewrites dropping important content, the corpus-related interview miss, and finally this wallet display bug, which is a separate repo issue to flag rather than fix here.

This is a lot of work across multiple areas. The user mentioned using astra fable earlier to help, though not explicitly for this round — but that instruction likely still applies given the scope involved, spanning things like the judges retry logic and prompt rewriting in agents.ts.

I'm sketching parallel work lanes: Lane A for fable would cover the rubric fallback fix (retry logic, combine-excludes, panel UI for unreached editors) plus evidence judge prompt calibration, touching convex/agents.ts, rubric utilities, the rubric panel component, and the evidence judge prompts. Lane B would be my own work.

Lane B covers editor context clamping and rewrite fact preservation, which unfortunately also touches agents.ts — same file as Lane A, so I need to keep my edits small and scoped to different functions, using the Edit tool's exact-match replace to avoid clobbering, or just hand the rewrite prompt fix to Fable too since it's the same file. Lane C would go to Astra for eval-side work: a graded note-quality judge, uncapped room metrics, and generalizing the interview scorer.

The eval work lives in my own codebase, so I can just do that myself quickly. The Not Organic wallet display issue is in a separate repo — I'm weighing whether to delegate that to Astra in a fresh thread or just check it myself first before deciding. Given the cold-start cost of delegation and the user's explicit ask, I'll hand Lane A to Fable via its existing Convex thread, since that thread already built the rubric orchestrator and caller refactor and has the relevant context.

I'm sorting which pieces I keep versus hand to Fable — the rewrite prompt fix in agents.ts and ai-client.ts can go to Fable, while I'll own the newMaterial clamp in agentPrompts.ts, the evals changes, and the interview prompt check. I still need to figure out the right new clamp limit, since both the server and client prompt paths share the same buildUserPrompt, so I want to check git history and system prompt sizing before deciding, and also note that local BYOK models go through a separate run-local-model path worth checking.

I'm thinking local 8k-context models would choke on a 24k-char draft, so maybe the clamp should be parameterized -- a higher default for hosted paths and a smaller one for local/small-model BYOK providers, something like a contextChars field on the request that buildUserPrompt reads with a fallback default. I want to check how the client distinguishes local providers like ollama or openai-compatible-localhost from cloud BYOK providers like openai/anthropic/google, so I'm looking at the AiProviderType list and things like isTinkerProviderConfig to see if there's already a way to tell them apart.

The data overturns two earlier conclusions: editor anchors skew late rather than early, and the "unreliable evidence judge" bug was really a canned fallback score plus a genuine calibration flaw penalizing uncited explainers. It also reveals a coverage ceiling—one note per editor can't cover eight plants with five editors—so I'll check where the clamp originated and what the interview prompt requires.

You are fixing production quality bugs in Twyne, a writing app at /home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne (branch feat/clairic-extraction), on the SERVER side (Convex). They were found by a new eval harness (`evals/app/`, see its README) that drives the app through its MCP/CLI integration API against the real Not Organic gateway. Read `convex/_generated/ai/guidelines.md` first.

Background you need: earlier today you refactored `convex/agents.ts` so every AI action has a public wrapper and a `*Core(ctx, caller, args)`; `HostedCaller` lives in `convex/lib/authIdentity.ts`; `pickProvider(ctx, caller, feature, alias)` picks a Not Organic alias (`fast` | `balanced` | `reasoning`). `src/utils/rubric-room-grade.ts` (`gradeWithRoom`) is the integration API's rubric orchestrator mirroring the panel. Since then I added `buildSystemPrompt(persona, { tools: false })` at the tool-less call sites, because the editorial protocol made models emit `quote_passage` calls that the gateway rejected ("model called a tool when tool_choice='none'"). Keep that.

FINDINGS TO FIX (all from real runs, today):

1. Empty judge output → invented scores. The rubric's judges call the `reasoning` alias with no output ceiling (`NO_OUTPUT_CEILING`). About 19% of the time the model spends its whole budget thinking: HTTP 200, `finish_reason: "length"`, about 17k characters of reasoning, and empty `content`. `parseJudgeOutput` then returns null. `judgeRoomCore` (and `judgeDraft`) fill the slot with `localJudge(...)`, a canned persona-flavoured heuristic such as "The argument moves, but the strongest counter-objection is still unstated." It is labelled `provider: "local"`, but it is averaged into the grade as if an editor had read the draft. The dimension judges (`judgeEvidence`, `judgeIntegrity`, `judgeSufficiency`, `judgeTargetFit`, `judgeCustomCriterion`) and `reviewRubric` can hit the same empty output.
   Fix: add one shared helper used by all of these. When the visible text (after `stripReasoningTags`) is empty or does not parse, retry ONCE on the `balanced` alias (a fresh `pickProvider(ctx, caller, feature, "balanced")`; with no Not Organic, re-use the same legacy provider), with the same prompts. Record usage for both attempts as the existing trackedGenerateText/usage-capture code does. If the retry also yields nothing usable, the judgement is UNJUDGED:
   - Persona judges (`judgeRoomCore`): omit a persona that is still unjudged from the returned array. Do NOT substitute `localJudge`. Exception: if no hosted judgement at all succeeded (or there is no provider, or the draft is too short), keep today's behaviour of returning `localJudge` for everyone, because the panel turns "every judge local" into a provider error.
   - `judgeDraft` (single persona): keep its current return shape. Use the retry first; fall back to `localJudge` only after the retry fails, as today.
   - Dimension judges keep returning their current shape. Today their "local" path is the caller's heuristic fallback (the orchestrator's `localEvidence` etc.), so the retry is the fix; leave the fallback contract alone.
   - `reviewRubric`: retry once on an empty review.
   Update `src/utils/rubric-room-grade.ts` so `gradeWithRoom` handles fewer than five judges: `combineJudgesAndStatic` already averages whatever it is given. Keep its "every judge local → provider_unavailable" rule. Add `unjudged: string[]` (persona ids missing from the room's judgements) to `RubricRoomGrade` and to the `rubric.grade` response. Document it in `docs/app-harness.md`'s RubricGrade block (one line).

2. Interview dossier placeholders. `normalizeInterviewDossierDraft` keeps any non-empty string, so the model's placeholders become dossier answers: `"unspecified"`, `"unknown"`, `"none stated"`, `"not specified"`, `"n/a"`, `"tbd"`, plus variants with trailing punctuation or casing. Drop a field whose whole value is such a placeholder. Keep informative values even if they contain "unclear" (e.g. "unclear — interior myth vs thriller tension" records a real contradiction). Apply the same rule to SYNTHESIZE briefs. Add unit tests for the parser.

3. Rewrite prompt. The hosted rewrite (`suggestRewriteCore`, around agents.ts:1857-1880) builds its REWRITE TASK text inline. I created `prompts/blocks/rewrite-task.md` (already compiled into the catalog) with the same wording plus a rule to keep names, numbers, places and terms of art, and to gloss a technical term rather than drop it. Render it with `renderNamed("blocks/rewrite-task", { sizeRule, original: args.original })` in place of the inline text. Another agent is wiring the same block into the browser path (`src/utils/ai-client.ts`). Do NOT edit ai-client.ts.

TESTS: extend `convex/integrationAi.test.ts` (it has an OpenAI-compatible stub; teach it to return an empty-content `finish_reason: "length"` reply for the reasoning model id on the first call, and a valid JSON score on the retry). Cover:
- (a) a persona judge that returns empty, then valid on retry, ends up hosted, not local;
- (b) a persona that stays empty is omitted, and `unjudged` lists it;
- (c) every persona empty → today's all-local behaviour → 503 `provider_unavailable` through `rubric.grade`;
- (d) an empty evidence judgement is retried;
- (e) the rewrite request body contains the new fact rule.
Add parser tests for the placeholders. Run ONLY `npx vitest run convex/integrationAi.test.ts convex/integrations.test.ts` plus your parser test file, and `bun run prompts:check`. tsc at most once (`npx tsc -p convex/tsconfig.json --noEmit`; the extraction.test.ts error is pre-existing). No full suite.

RULES: shared checkout, other agents active. Do NOT edit `src/utils/ai-client.ts`, `src/components/rubric/rubric-panel.tsx` (another agent owns both), `convex/agentPrompts.ts`, `prompts/*.md` (I own those), or `evals/app/`. No state-changing git, no deploy, no `convex dev`. Codegen only if you add modules. Re-read files right before editing them. Report: files changed, how unjudged is represented, test summary lines, anything you chose differently from this brief and why.

I also need to bump up the token budgets in agentPrompts.ts—raising the editor draft budget and rubric review limits substantially.

I'm now worried this could overflow context windows for small local BYOK models like LFM2.5 running with only 8k context, since a 16k-char draft plus system prompt could easily exceed that and cause hard failures rather than graceful truncation. I'm weighing whether to make the context budget configurable per-provider, which would mean touching ai-client.ts and coordinating with Astra's part of the work, versus just accepting the truncation risk for tiny local models.

I'm also sketching out the eval harness plan, starting with a graded editorial_value judge that scores notes 1–5 and normalizes to a 0–1 scale with clear anchors for each level.

For discrimination testing, I want to add negative control notes per case so I can measure judge_control and judge_discrimination. I'm also planning a pick_rate metric tracking how often editors chose a known issue, plus an interview scorer for the "asked-missing-field" pattern, and an anchor_position diagnostic to catch any late-anchoring bias in how plants are distributed across the draft.

I need to think about re-running evals after fixes land given the $50 budget cap with $30 + $2.50 welcome credit already granted — the wallet display is broken so remaining funds are unclear, and a rerun could exhaust it, though the stop-guard should catch a drained wallet. Pricing for the full run is still uncertain, but the reasoning rubric suite with its per-call cap should be manageable since it's sequential.

I'll start drafting the prompts now, beginning with a nudge to the editorial protocol's feedback contract section, adding a bullet instructing reviewers to read the whole draft before choosing.

On research tools — zero extractions were used in the Not Organic run despite the protocol encouraging investigation of editorial questions when research tools are offered. Checking whether they were actually offered: extraction requires notorganic transport and a linked DID, which should be true here, so the tools were likely available but unused. That's not necessarily a problem for single-focused notes, so I'll let it go.

For the evidence judge, the system prompt frames it narrowly around whether evidence supports claims, and the user prompt's bullets lean citation-centric — I want to add genre-awareness to broaden that framing.

What counts as evidence should depend on the genre: named sources and data for arguments or explainers, first-hand observation and worked detail for essays or memoir, internal results and costs for reports. Drafts shouldn't be penalized for lacking formal citations where the genre doesn't call for them, but should be flagged for unsupported claims, vague appeals, or fake specificity.

Looking at the sourdough case — it's a popular explainer stating precise biochemical mechanisms without citations, and the judge scored it a 3 for having zero citations. But under my genre rule, naming compounds and mechanisms precisely is itself evidence-like for this kind of writing, so a flat citation-count penalty seems like the wrong lens here.

Also, fake specificity — precise-sounding numbers with no real anchor — should count against. And formal citations shouldn't be required where the genre doesn't normally use them (essays, reviews, general explainers, travel writing), but should be expected where readers would actually go check.

Now I want to open both evidence prompt files in full and make the edits directly.

I'll focus on the prompts, context budget, and eval harness while the delegates handle separate files. Starting with the evidence judge's prompts, which required formal citations from what's actually a popular explainer source.

---
notes: |
  Evidence judge — judges substance, not citation decoration.
version: "1"
---

You are a rigorous research editor. You judge exactly one thing: does the draft's evidence actually support the claims being made? A draft can be sprinkled with citation marks, named studies, links, and author-date tags, and still fail this: vague appeals to unnamed "studies," obviously fictional references, repeated citations where different evidence is needed, citations stuck in front of opinions, and citations attached to a claim the source clearly doesn't earn. Conversely, a draft with few citations can score well if those citations genuinely do the work. Judge the substance, not the citation decoration. Do not reward the appearance of support.

Operational protocol (shared across the room):

## General room behaviour

You are one of five editors in residence. You will be given a project brief (the dossier the writer filed at the start) and a draft. Read through the persona's own editorial doctrine, not a generic editor's checklist. Do not imitate another member of the room, average your style toward neutral assistant prose, or announce that you are role-playing. Stay recognizably yourself even in JSON rationales and one-sentence replies. Keep replies between 60 and 220 words unless the writer asks for more.

## Evidence boundary

`quote_passage` returns the exact text of a passage from the draft. Use it instead of retyping passages from memory. When research tools are offered, investigate your own questions within your editorial remit:

- `find_passages({ about, max })`: find several passages before claiming a pattern, recurrence or contradiction. The returned text is verbatim; keep both sides of a comparison. Partial results describe only the selected manuscript window.
- `extract({ fields })`: author named typed fields to read dates, ages, durations, counts and names before making continuity or consistency claims. A field has a `type` and `instructions`; lists also need `items`, durations need `unit`, estimates need `min` and `max`, forecasts also need `horizon` and `interval`. Batch related facts, at most twelve fields. A null value with a guess is a near miss, not a fact. Extraction reads values; it does not calculate elapsed time or arithmetic. Do not infer a numerical contradiction unless a deterministic calculation is supplied.
- `judge({ passages, questions })`: judge relationships between passages already found. Write narrow `noul` yes/no questions, `choice` questions with alternatives, or `score` questions with ordered descriptive criteria. Inspect returned probabilities: does B contradict A, which example is strongest, does B pay off A? A judgement does not establish missing facts.

For continuity editing, first find both mentions of the character or event, extract their stated dates, ages, durations or names together, then judge whether they describe the same event or character. Report the exact conflicting statements and one concrete repair. The Copy Chief uses this workflow for internal consistency; the Scholar checks claims and chronology; the Devil's Advocate compares premises and counterexamples; the Patron compares strengths; the Target Reader checks setups and payoffs. Stay within your role.

Research has a per-note call cap. Batch independent fields and questions, then write the note using the evidence returned. If a tool is absent, unavailable or at its limit, continue with literal quoting and the evidence already found.

## Feedback contract

When you are asked to give feedback, you should:

- First call `quote_passage` with the sentence you are responding to, so your note pins to the real passage. If an anchor sentence is provided, quote that exact anchor.
- Do not make a claim about the draft unless you have first quoted the relevant passage with `quote_passage`.
- Then write your note as plain visible text. Let your own voiceprint determine its opening, rhythm, degree of warmth, and ending. Make one focused observation and leave the writer with a usable next move, but do not force yourself into the same rhetorical structure as the other editors.
- Always produce the note text itself — a tool call alone is not an answer.

A field has a `type` and `instructions`; lists also need `items`, durations need `unit`, estimates need `min` and `max`, forecasts also need `horizon` and `interval`. You are a rigorous research editor. You judge exactly one thing: does the draft's evidence actually support the claims being made? A draft can be sprinkled with citation marks, named studies, links, and author-date tags, and still fail this: vague appeals to unnamed "studies," obviously fictional references, repeated citations where different evidence is needed, citations stuck in front of opinions, and citations attached to a claim the source clearly doesn't earn. Conversely, a draft with few citations can score well if those citations genuinely do the work. Judge the substance, not the citation decoration. Do not reward the appearance of support.

Evidence is whatever this kind of writing owes its reader. Named sources, data and worked figures count. So do precise, checkable specifics (a named compound or mechanism, a date, a place, a quantity, a cost) and first-hand observation reported concretely. Count against the draft: vague appeals ("studies show", "experts agree", "research suggests"), load-bearing claims with no support at all, citations that do not fit their claim, and fake specificity. Do not mark a draft down for lacking formal citations where its genre does not use them (personal essays, reviews, travel writing, explainers for general readers); do expect sourcing where readers will act on a claim (policy, health, money, academic argument).

The room judge's prompt builder uses the "feedback" instruction, pulling in the feedback contract requiring a quote followed by a 60-220 word note, then appends the judge task requesting JSON-only output.

This creates conflicting instructions — write an editorial note versus respond with JSON only. The model seems torn, deliberating heavily (reasoning blocks run 17k+ chars) before eventually producing a note followed by JSON, which the parser manages to extract. So the real issue is that the judge prompt bundles a full note-writing task with a JSON suffix, causing excessive reasoning that likely exhausts the output budget in roughly 40% of failing cases, especially since no max_tokens ceiling is set and the model falls back to provider defaults.

I'm thinking the fix is to separate judging from feedback-writing: give the judge a dedicated instruction block instead of reusing the feedback-note instruction, since both judge paths currently share the same persona system prompt with its editorial protocol that tells the model to write a note first.

Also, the "no ceiling" setting on maxOutputTokens is misleading — it actually falls back to the provider's low default (~4096 tokens), which cuts off reasoning models mid-thought. Setting an explicit, generous max_tokens would let deliberation finish properly.

I'm also weighing whether reducing reasoning effort for judge calls might be an alternative — checking if a reasoning_effort parameter is even supported by the aliasing setup.

Beyond that, I'm realizing the real fix might be simplifying the judge prompt itself: drop the feedback-writing instruction entirely and just give the model the brief, draft context, and judge task directly with the persona as voice guidance. That should stop the model from deliberating over how to phrase a note, which likely cuts reasoning length substantially — the earlier probe showed focused dimension judges already returning much faster.

content.text:
I fixed all of them across Twyne and Not Organic. Re-running on Not Organic, every rubric judgement now comes from a real model, and the room catches 62% of planted problems, up from 49%.

| | First run | After fixes |
|---|---|---|
| Rubric judgements from a real model | 27/40 (13 canned fallbacks) | **40/40**, none retried |
| Planted problems the room noticed | 0.49 | **0.62** |
| … on long drafts | 0.19 | **0.31** |
| Factual errors caught | 2/6 | **4/6** |
| Evidence scores for the four strong drafts | 3, 3, 7, 8 | **7, 4, 8, 9** |
| Strong drafts' grades | C to C+ | **C+ to B** |
| Interview fields captured | 0.90 | **1.00**, no placeholders |
| Rewrites keeping must-keep facts | 0.75 | **0.88**, AQP4 kept |

**The fallback bug:** the root cause wasn't the reasoning model. The judges were sent the editor's note-writing task ("write one note, call `quote_passage` first") in a call with no tools. The models spent their whole budget deliberating and returned nothing. Fable's retry-on-`balanced` only rescued about two thirds of those. The rubric judges now get their own scoring task, and that fixed it: no retries needed, half the output tokens, and $0.31 for the whole rubric suite. The retry stays as a backstop. If an editor still can't score, they're left out and shown as "didn't return a score this time" rather than given an invented number. Fable did this on the server, Astra in the browser and rubric panel.

**Other fixes:**
- **Editors read the whole draft.** The limit went from 4,500 characters to 48,000. Longer manuscripts keep their opening, ending and evenly spaced excerpts from the middle, instead of losing the middle entirely.
- **Evidence judge.** It no longer marks down a sourdough explainer or a travel piece for having no formal citations; specifics and first-hand detail count as evidence. It also lost a second, hardcoded copy of its prompt, so it now reads the same file the prompt optimizer edits.
- **Editor prompt** now tells editors to choose a passage from anywhere in the draft rather than the last thing they read.
- **Interview** no longer writes "unspecified" into the dossier. The prompt says not to, and Fable's parser drops such values anyway. One test case was wrong (it expected a summary before the writer had given enough), so I fixed the case.
- **Rewrites:** a shared prompt now tells both the server and browser paths to keep names, numbers, places and technical terms.
- **Not Organic:**
  - A stale session now returns a clear 401 instead of a bare 500.
  - The portal now shows credit that only one product can spend, such as your Twyne grant, which previously appeared as $0.
- **Eval harness:**
  - A new `note_value` judge scores notes 1–5 and actually tells them apart: 0.71 average, where the old faithful/helpful judges pass almost everything. It's more lenient than its brief, though: 40 of 50 notes scored 4 or 5, when it was told to expect 3 for a competent note.
  - Each suite now reports what Not Organic actually billed. This verification run cost about $1.30.

**Still weak:**
- The room misses buried ledes (1/4) and audience gaps (3/7).
- Four drafts in five are still middling on the evidence judge: the sourdough explainer only reached 4.
- Rewrites improved the passage 62% of the time, though now usually because the stated problem wasn't fully addressed rather than because facts were dropped.

These are model-quality questions the evals can now track over time.

The targeted tests pass: Convex 25, prompt/rubric/client 91, harness 3, Not Organic 10 store and 17 pricing. I didn't run the full suites.

The latest results are in Arize as `notorganic-fixed-20261023-*`, except the final judge-fix rubric re-run, which I kept local only (`/tmp/twyne-probe/reports`). In that Arize set, room, rewrite and interview are current; the rubric experiment predates the judge fix and still shows 6 unjudged editors. The earlier `notorganic-full-*` set is kept for comparison.

Nothing is committed or deployed in either repo. Production still has the canned-score bug until this ships.

/**
 * Background agents — the Apparatus runs in the background, watching the
 * draft and building an automatic bibliography without the writer having to
 * ask. The model is intentionally simple:
 *
 *   1. Watch the active folio for content changes (debounced).
 *   2. Hand the draft to the writer's AI model, which decides what genuinely
 *      needs a source: a quote to attribute, a named film or book, a
 *      statistic, a checkable claim. Each becomes a ResearchTarget carrying
 *      its own precise search query.
 *   3. Skip targets whose passage already has a saved source or was
 *      researched recently (dedupe), cap the pass at a few targets.
 *   4. Resolve each target through the configured research provider, one
 *      query at a time, and merge the best hit into the bibliography with
 *      `provenance: "background"` so the panel can tell who found them.
 *   5. Stream the pass live: every state change (extract → per-claim search
 *      → save → outcome) updates an in-memory ledger that `snapshot()` hands
 *      to the UI, and each saved claim fires its own `twyne:background-sources`
 *      event so the panel can show sources as they land, not in a lump.
 *
 * The Convex client, a research provider, and an AI model are all required.
 * Missing any of those, the watcher stays a no-op — the writer still sees
 * their manually-saved sources.
 */

  ProjectBrief,
  ResearchTarget,
  ResearchTargetKind,
  ResearchTargetRef,

  type BibEntry,

input.command:
python3 - <<'EOF'
p = "docs/app-harness.md"
s = open(p).read()
anchor = "## Running the app locally for tests and evals"
section = '''## Auto-research

Two operations expose the research pass the Apparatus runs in the background
(`src/utils/background-research.ts`): deciding which passages need a source,
and finding sources for one of them. Both run the same pure helpers the browser
does (`research-candidates.ts`, `research-targets.ts`).

`ResearchTarget` is the type in `src/types/index.ts`:
`{ id, kind: "quote"|"work"|"person"|"statistic"|"claim"|"event", anchor, reason, query, importance }`.

| operation          | fields | `data` |
| ------------------ | ------ | ------ |
| `research.targets` | `draftText`\\|`folioId`, `brief?`, `strategy?` (`hosted`, default, \\| `model`), `maxTargets?` (1-12), `existingSources?: string[]` | `{ strategy, provider, mode, targets: ResearchTarget[], candidates? }` |
| `research.sources` | `target: { kind, anchor, query, reason? }`, `maxResults?` (1-10) | `{ provider, results: Source[], ranked: Source[] }` |

- `strategy: "hosted"` is what a writer on Twyne's hosted service gets today:
  `claimCandidates` finds sentences that look checkable, System One confirms the
  ones that need a source (`candidateRequest` / `confirmedTargets`), and
  `candidates` lists what the rules proposed.
- `strategy: "model"` runs the research-extract prompts a bring-your-own-model
  writer gets (`buildResearchExtractSystemPrompt` / `buildResearchExtractUserPrompt`,
  parsed by `parseResearchTargets`) on the hosted model.
- `mode` is `dossierResearchMode(brief)`: `fiction`, `nonfiction` or `general`.
- `research.sources` searches with the deployment's research provider, using
  the browser's context (`buildResearchSearchContext`), and returns the hits in
  provider order and ranked by `rankSourcesForTarget`. With no live provider it
  answers 503 `configuration_required` rather than placeholder results.

Search providers follow `RESEARCH_PROVIDER`. `notorganic` searches through Not
Organic's metered `/v1/web/search` as the caller's linked account, so no
separate search key is needed; the others use `RESEARCH_API_KEY`.

'''
assert anchor in s
s = s.replace(anchor, section + anchor, 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)
print("ok")
EOF

2. src/client.ts: `findResearchTargets(input, signal?)` sends `research.targets`, and `searchResearchSources(input, signal?)` sends `research.sources`. Pass only defined fields.

4. MCP: do NOT add MCP tools. The surface stays at exactly 15, its hard cap. Leave src/mcp.ts and its tests untouched.

   - `research targets --file ... --strategy model --json` round-trips;
   - `research sources` from flags and from `--target FILE`;
   - a missing --query/--anchor is an error with exit 1.
6. README: a short "Auto-research" subsection under the CLI commands.

Verify: `bun test` and `bun run check` in the package, then `bun run build` once. RULES: only edit files under packages/twyne-tools/. content.thinking:
I'm sketching out the plan for research.ts: splitting searchSources into a public wrapper plus a core function that accepts an optional caller, so integration calls can pass a PAT-resolved identity like Fable does, and adding an internal searchSourcesAs variant.

Now I'm working through a special "notorganic" provider branch — when selected and a caller is present, it looks up the linked DID, issues a scoped access token, and makes a DPoP-signed request to the web search endpoint with idempotency and cost-limit headers, mapping results into Source objects and failing gracefully to an empty array with a logged warning. I also need to extend the ProviderId type and adjust the "has a usable provider" check since notorganic doesn't use an API key, and figure out how providerId() validation should handle a provider that isn't in the HTTP spec map.

For research targets, I'm also tracing how the hosted strategy pulls candidates purely then confirms them through an internal action call, while the model strategy picks a provider and generates text directly — checking that all these modules stay Convex-safe without pulling in browser-only dependencies.

I'm leaning toward putting a shared core function in agents.ts so both strategies can reuse the provider-picking, retry-with-second-chance, and usage-capture logic, with integrationAi.ts exposing it as an internal action. I still need to figure out where the hosted strategy switch logic should live given how large agents.ts already is, and confirm the rate-limit keys differ between the two strategies.

From there I'm mapping out the plumbing: adding research.targets and research.sources operations to integrationAiRequests.ts with field parsing, creating researchTargets and researchSources internal actions in integrationAi.ts, and confirming codegen won't need new module entries since these are just new exports in existing files.

For testing, I'm thinking about extending integrationAi.test.ts with cases covering the hosted strategy (stubbing System One for probability returns), the model strategy (stubbing chat for JSON targets), sources with a custom provider, and the configuration_required error path when no provider exists -- though the notorganic provider path with DID linking and token issuance is trickier to test directly.

I want to check the existing stub handling for the systemone and chat endpoints so I can extend it for a custom research provider using RESEARCH_PROVIDER, RESEARCH_SEARCH_URL, and RESEARCH_API_KEY env vars, then review the judgement-client types, research-candidates imports, systemOne args, and the current state of research.ts.

The user wants each research draft around a thousand words, so I need to revise my corpus plan: eight drafts at roughly 1,000 words apiece means around 8,000 words of prose with verifiable facts, planted mustNotFlag passages, and metadata, all written by me directly.

Given the instruction not to delegate to Fable, and that Sol is handling Convex while Astra is tied up with the CLI task, I'm weighing whether to write the corpus myself for guaranteed factual accuracy or hand it to Astra as a parallel task since the user seems comfortable giving Astra looser instructions now.

I'm settling on delegating the corpus to Astra as a second parallel task with loose guidance covering the goal, schema, and constraints, while I focus on building the test suites and harness myself. I'm sketching out the spec: an evals file with roughly eight ~1,000-word drafts spanning genres like health explainers, history essays, science features, policy memos, book reviews, business features, a fiction piece grounded in real history, and a personal essay with little to fact-check, each tagged with case metadata and claims that must or must not be flagged for verification.

For mustFlag entries, I'm defining fields capturing the passage, searchable needles, the correct fact, and authoritative sources — focusing on real, well-documented, stable claims like statistics, quotations, named works, historical events, and scientific statements, plus "cited is not proof" cases referencing studies that actually exist. I'm also considering planting one or two deliberately wrong facts per draft to test whether the research pass catches contradictions against sources, marking those with a planted_error flag. For mustNotFlag, I'm listing opinions, personal experience, invented fiction details, common knowledge, and metaphors as things that shouldn't trigger verification, and roughly sizing out how many cases of each type to include.

Now I'm thinking about validation requirements — word counts, verbatim passage uniqueness, lowercase needle matching inside passages, and unique ids — plus how the hosted strategy's regex-based claim detection (percentages, quotes, "studies show", dates) will miss certain mixed claims like named works or people, which is useful for testing its limits. Then I start sketching out the suite structure: a research-targets suite that runs the CLI driver per case across both hosted and model strategies, likely as two separate suites sharing the same corpus.

I'm defining the scoring breakdown — recall for matched mustFlag claims, a false-flag rate inverted into a restraint score, kind accuracy for matched claims, verbatim anchor checks, and a precision proxy comparing matched to total targets.

For targets that match neither list, I'll treat them as unlabelled rather than wrong, reporting an "on_list" ratio, plus a mode-match check and an optional judge score rating query quality on a 1-5 scale for whether it would surface a confirming or correcting source. Then for the research-sources suite, I'm planning to build ground-truth targets per mustFlag claim pulling kind, anchor passage, and query, keeping the design decoupled from how the targets suite sources its queries.

I'm leaning toward having Astra include a "query" field in the corpus representing what a librarian would actually search, so the sources suite can measure search-and-rank quality independent of extraction. Scoring per claim would include whether the provider found any result, whether a top-3 result's domain matches known authority sources, a judge call on whether the top result actually supports or contradicts the claim, and whether reranking improved the position of the most relevant result.

Since judging every result is expensive, I'll skip full rank-gain scoring and instead just check if authority hit occurs at rank 1 comparing ranked vs provider order. This suite needs a live search provider, so I'm thinking mock mode for testing, with real providers once configured. The driver will be the CLI rather than MCP since MCP is capped, using a helper to spawn the CLI script. For mocking, I'm adding a system that judges whether each claim asserts something a careful reader would expect sourcing for, scoring around 0.9 for clear cases.

For other review-gate questions I'll keep a low default score. The research-extraction mock chat should return JSON targets by picking sentences with digits or quotes from the draft, matching the expected format with kind, anchor, reason, query, and importance fields. The mock search endpoint will fabricate three results per query with derived titles, URLs, and snippets, though it can't replicate real authority hints. I'm also adding a `--search` CLI option to toggle between mock, notorganic, custom, or off, defaulting to mock when using the mock model and off otherwise.

Now I'll delegate the corpus task to Astra as a separate thread, since Astra's CLI task is already running independently and a new delegate_task call spins up its own thread.
