Write an evaluation corpus for Twyne's auto-research. Twyne is a writing app (repo: /home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne). As the writer drafts, a background agent decides which passages need a source and searches for one. Read `prompts/research-extract-system.md` (the model strategy's instructions) and `src/utils/research-candidates.ts` (the rule-based strategy hosted writers get). The corpus has to measure both: what gets flagged, what gets wrongly flagged, and whether search finds a source that settles each claim.

Write `evals/app/cases/research.jsonl`: 8 drafts of about 1,000 words each (900 to 1,100), as real, competent prose in varied genres:
- nonfiction (a health or science explainer, a history essay, a policy memo, a book review that quotes its subject, a tech or business feature);
- at least one fiction piece built on real history, where the real scaffolding needs checking and the invented story doesn't;
- one personal essay with almost nothing checkable, to test restraint.

Every flagged claim must be REAL and well documented, so a search engine can find a source that settles it. Use stable, encyclopedic facts, and exact wording for any quotation. One or two drafts may carry a single planted error (a wrong date or figure); record the correct fact and mark it.

Each line:
`{"case_id","genre","mode":"fiction|nonfiction|general","brief":{"answers":{"workingTitle","format","audience","goal","tone","constraints","successSignal"},"attachments":[],"completedAt":1790000000000,"updatedAt":1790000000000},"draftText","mustFlag":[{"id","kind":"quote|work|person|statistic|claim|event","passage","needles":[…],"fact","query","sources":[…],"plantedError"?:true}],"mustNotFlag":[{"id","why":"opinion|experience|invented|common-knowledge|metaphor","passage","needles":[…]}]}`

- `passage`: a verbatim substring of draftText, appearing exactly once.
- `needles`: 1-3 lowercase words or short phrases. A target whose anchor or query contains all of them is that claim; every needle must also appear in the passage.
- `fact`: the true statement, in one sentence.
- `query`: the search query a good research librarian would write for this claim.
- `sources`: domains or title fragments of sources that establish the fact (e.g. "britannica.com", "who.int", "nobelprize.org").
- Aim for about 5-7 mustFlag and 3-4 mustNotFlag per draft, and spread the kinds. Include cases the regex rules in research-candidates.ts will miss (named works, people in context, unattributed claims) and cases they will catch (percentages, "studies show", dated events, attributed quotes).

Also add a short `evals/app/cases/README.md` section describing the file. Validate with a script you keep in /tmp (word counts, verbatim-once passages, needles inside passages, unique ids). Only create these two files: other agents are working in this checkout, so touch nothing else and run no state-changing git. Report the validation output and a table of case, genre, word count, and flag counts.

Base directory for this skill: /home/diogenes/.claude/plugins/cache/typesafe-ai/typesafe/0.5.7/skills/typesafe-ai

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe makes units of AI intelligence usable like programming primitives: small
judgments you can compose into larger capabilities. Its **System One models** return
fast, focused judgments that software can consume directly. **Jev** is TypeSafe's
flagship and first System One model. It understands natural language and returns
typed answers and probabilities rather
than generating text or reasoning explanations. Code owns the workflow; the model
supplies programmable common sense where ordinary code needs semantic understanding.

## Read the live docs

**The live TypeSafe docs are the source of truth. Read them as part of the task.**
This skill gives direction; the docs carry current concepts, prompting guidance,
API contracts, SDK usage, models, limits, and worked examples.

- Start with the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt) to discover
  relevant pages and cookbooks. Use targeted reads rather than loading the entire site.
- Mintlify serves Markdown by appending `.md` to a page path, for example
  [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md).
  Follow links from the index; convert extensionless documentation page links to
  `.md` when useful. Resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Before writing an integration, read the current API or chosen SDK page and the
  question guidance relevant to the design. For a new workflow, also inspect the
  closest cookbook: it often shows a better decomposition than a generic classifier.
- If the index is unavailable, use the direct links below or the site's navigation.
  If Markdown fetching fails, try the normal page. If live access is unavailable,
  use available local docs or installed SDK types, state that limitation, and avoid
  inventing version-dependent details.

| Task | Start here; follow the relevant details |
| --- | --- |
| Understand the programming model | [System One](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/system-one.md), [building guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/how-to-build-with-system-one.md) |
| Explore what to build | [Use-case map](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/use-case-map.md), then relevant cookbooks from the index |
| Prepare inputs and questions | [State](https://docs.typesafe.ai/concepts/state.md), [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives.md), then the chosen primitive's page |
| Decide how to handle uncertainty | [Confidence](https://docs.typesafe.ai/confidence.md) |
| Write API code | [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/api.md), [Python SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/python.md), or [JavaScript SDK](https://docs.typesafe.ai/sdk/javascript.md) |
| Update an older integration | [Migration guide](https://docs.typesafe.ai/migrating-to-v1.md) and the installed SDK's current reference |

## Find the useful shape

Start from the behavior the user wants: what will the application show, select,
change, or hand off? Work backward to the judgments it needs. Keep known rules,
calculations, exact lookups, and execution in code. Preserve the user's chosen stack
and scope; add TypeSafe where semantic understanding helps.

When brainstorming or choosing an architecture, consider more than classification.
The patterns below are starting points: combine primitives around the user's goal,
including ideas that do not fit an established recipe.

- **Route and fill known arguments.** A request can select a handler and its typed
  parameters. Ask useful branch-specific questions up front and consume only the
  relevant answers. Explore [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md)
  and [speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Find candidate values or source spans in code,
  use a judgment to select the intended one, then copy or normalize it. Code can
  also assemble source text into a formatted document or reading guide. Explore
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md)
  and [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates, compare their relevance to a
  query, and select useful context. Explore [reranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md)
  and [hierarchical classification](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/hierarchical_classification.md).
- **Turn judgments into reusable data.** Score dimensions once, then let code or
  user controls change weights, thresholds, rankings, and views. With labeled
  outcomes, those signals can become classical ML features. Explore

| Need | Primitive | Important distinction |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One of a defined set | [Choice](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/choice.md) | Picks one option; its distribution compares competing options |
| Whether a condition holds | [Noul](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/noul.md) | Probability of yes; no separate confidence; use one per label when several may apply |
| Degree along a described dimension | [Score](https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives/score.md) | Probability-weighted position on ordered levels; use comparable per-item Scores for graded ranking |

assert old in s; s = s.replace(old, new, 1)
open(p, "w").write(s)

p = "evals/app/README.md"

open(p, "w").write(s)
print("ok")
EOF

content.content:
# Citation-Check Pattern Summary

**State structure.** Each model call receives a two-field state: `claim` (the LLM's assertion) and `section` (the source text that gets judged). The section comes from one of two places:
- The numbered section where an exact string match located the quote.
- The section the citation names, when the citation has no quote ("section-only").

**Step 1: string match, no model.** Whitespace is collapsed and curly quotes are straightened. The quote is then searched for as a substring across the sections.
- If the quote isn't found, the citation is labeled `fabricated` immediately, with no confidence score.
- The match is exact after normalization, so truncated or reworded quotes also land as fabricated. The authors note that production use would need fuzzy matching.

**Step 2: one `Choice` question.** It is called via `client.system_one(state=..., questions=QUESTIONS, model="jev-1.12")`. The definition, verbatim:

- instructions: "How does the section relate to the claim?"
- `supports`: "The section states the claim or directly implies that it is true"
- `contradicts`: "The section states the opposite of the claim or implies it is false"
- `says_nothing`: "The section does not address what the claim asserts, either way"

**Composing the verdict.** The highest-probability option is mapped to a label:
- supports → `verified`
- contradicts → `contradicted`
- says_nothing → `unsupported`

Combined with the fabricated case, `check_citation()` returns one of four labels, plus the confidence and an auto/review flag.

**Threshold.** `AUTO_ACCEPT = 0.8`.
- At or above 0.8, the verdict is accepted automatically.
- Below 0.8, a person confirms it first.
- The advice is to begin strict and loosen the threshold as you gain trust in the model on your own documents.

In the RFC 7519 demo, the four accurate citations scored 0.93 or higher. The contradicted one scored 0.99. The two unsupported ones (0.27, 0.56) went to review.

**Batching.** The page never states a per-request limit. The example sends just one question per citation, with one request per surviving citation. The "twelve fields per request" cap in the extra context you included belongs to a separate learning-extraction feature, not this API.

# TypeSafe Score Questions: Summary

**A note on the JSON examples:** I can't reproduce the full JSON blocks verbatim because each one is far longer than the 125-character quote limit. Below I quote short fragments exactly and describe the rest in my own words. Also, the page never shows the raw request JSON. It links to the Playground and gives a Python SDK example instead.

## Request shape

The POST body has three top-level fields: `state` (the content to rate), `model`, and `questions`. You can send it to `https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` or use the SDK's `system_one` method.

Each Score question, keyed by an id you pick (the model never sees the id), contains:
- **`type`**: `"score"`.
- **`instructions`**: what the model is rating, e.g. `"How severe is the reported issue?"`
- **`criteria`**: an ordered list of level descriptions, running from the low end to the high end. A level's number is its index, starting at 0.

`instructions` and each level may be a string, an object, or an array. Start with strings. Switch to objects when a level needs a description plus example situations, and use identical field names on every level. The structured example uses fields `what` and `examples`, e.g. `"what": "Cosmetic; no impact to functionality"`.

## Response contents

Answers come back under the same ids. Short excerpts from the bug-severity response:
- `"type": "score",`
- `"score": 1.43,`
- `"confidence": 0.35,`
- `legend`, which maps each level number back to its description, e.g. `"1": "Broken or degraded feature, but workaround exists",`
- `probabilities`, one per level and keyed by string, summing to 1: `"0": 0.0,` / `"1": 0.57,` / `"2": 0.43`

The response also includes `model` (e.g. `"jev-1.13.0"`) and `usage` token counts. The Python SDK keys `probabilities` and `legend` by integer instead of string.

**Score as an expected value:** the doc doesn't use the term "expected value," but the score is exactly that. Each level number is weighted by its probability and the results are summed: "0 x 0.0 + 1 x 0.57 + 2 x 0.43 = 1.43". It ranges from 0 up to the top level number and can fall between levels.

**Confidence:** a value from 0 to 1 based on how spread out the probabilities are. All probability on one level gives 1.0. The doc warns this reflects the model's answer, "not a guarantee that the answer is correct."

## Number of levels

- At least two levels; the API caps it at 10.
- Use as many levels as you can make genuinely distinct. "Three is fine." Don't add levels you can't tell apart.
- If a rare extreme at the top needs different handling, give it a separate level (e.g. "abusive or threatening").

## Writing good level descriptions

- **Describe situations, not degrees.** "Moderately severe" gives the model nothing to match against.
- **Each level stands alone.** The model can't see a level's number or its neighbours, so relative wording or numbers don't help. With criteria of just `["0", "1", "2"]`, a clearly cosmetic bug scored 0.55 at confidence 0.33.
- **Measure one dimension per question.** If a level combines several traits, split it into separate Score questions and combine them in code.
- **If there's no in-between,** use a Choice or several Noul questions instead.
- **Choose examples carefully.** Only examples that resemble your real inputs help. In the doc's test, an unrelated example changed nothing.
- **Validate.** Test against inputs whose correct level you already know. Higher confidence alone doesn't prove a description is better.

## Comparing scores across items

- A fractional score works for ranking items, or you can round it when you need a single outcome.
- The same score can come from different distributions. For example, 1.0 could be all probability on level 1, or half on level 0 and half on level 2. Check `probabilities` and `confidence` alongside the score.
- Low confidence usually means the levels overlap for that input, the question mixes several dimensions, or the input lacks enough information.
- To combine scales of different lengths, first normalize each score by dividing by its top level number, `len(criteria) - 1`. Then apply your own weights. The doc's example: `0.6 × 0.62 + 0.3 × 0.64 + 0.1 × 1.0 = 0.664`. This approach is the "Composite scoring" pattern.
- Send multiple Score questions in one request. They run in parallel, adding little latency and only a few extra tokens.

content.content:
# TypeSafe System One: HTTP API Contract

Some JSON examples are shown as excerpts so that each quote stays under 125 characters.

## Endpoint and Auth
- **Endpoint:** `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone`
- **Auth header:** `Authorization: Bearer <API_KEY>` (HTTP bearer scheme)
- **Discover models:** `GET /v1/models`
- **Optional headers:** Both accept only the value `'true'`.
  - `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images` is required for image assets or box questions.
  - `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context` enables long context.
- **Content types:** `application/json`, or `multipart/form-data`. In multipart, the JSON goes first as a part named `request`, followed by one uniquely named part per image.

## Request Fields
| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | yes | Model name or alias, e.g. `jev-latest` |
| `state` | yes | A string, object, or array. Every question refers to this content. |
| `questions` | yes | An object of named questions, with at least 1 |
| `assets` | no | Images keyed by placeholders. Each placeholder in strings is swapped for its image. Requires a vision-language model. |

Example question: `"billing": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is this message about billing?"}`

## Question Types and Limits
- **noul:** A yes/no question. `instructions` and `criteria` (`true`/`false`) are both optional.
- **choice:** `criteria` is required and maps choice names to descriptions, with **1–255** entries.
- **score:** `criteria` is required and is an ordered array of **1–10** levels. Scoring starts at 0.
- **box:** Locates something in an image. Requires the Images header.

**Not in the document:**
- A maximum number of questions per request. Only a minimum of 1 is specified.
- A maximum state size or token limit.

## Response
The response has three top-level fields:
- `model`, which may differ from the alias you sent
- `answers`, keyed by your question names
- `usage`, e.g. `{"input_tokens": 120, "output_tokens": 12}`. Output tokens are "currently free of charge."

### noul
Returns a probability of yes/true between 0 and 1.

`"billing": {"type": "noul", "noul": 0.98}`

### choice
Returns `choice` (the option with the highest probability), `confidence`, and `probabilities`. The probabilities sum to roughly 1.

- `"choice": "calm", "confidence": 0.7`
- `"probabilities": {"angry": 0.15, "calm": 0.8, "excited": 0.05}`

### score
Returns `score` (a probability-weighted expected value, which can fall between levels), `confidence`, `legend`, and `probabilities`.

- `"score": 1.7, "confidence": 0.55`
- `{"0": "Can wait", "1": "Needs attention this week", "2": "Needs attention today"}`
- `{"0": 0.1, "1": 0.1, "2": 0.8}`

### box
Returns edges as fractions from 0 to 1, measured from the top and left. `confidence` may be null.

`"box": {"top": 0.2, "bottom": 0.66, "left": 0.19, "right": 0.68}, "confidence": null`

## Errors
- **200:** Success.
- **422:** Validation error. The `detail[]` array contains `loc`, `msg`, and `type` (required), plus optional `input` and `ctx`.
  - Example: `{"loc": ["body", "state"], "msg": "Field required", "type": "missing"}`
- No other status codes (401, 429, 5xx) are documented.

## Rate Limits
The document does not specify any.

The extra context you supplied describes a different system. Its "four requests per minute" limit does not apply to this API.

  - `TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context` enables long context.
- **Content types:** `application/json`, or `multipart/form-data`. In multipart, the JSON goes first as a part named `request`, followed by one uniquely named part per image.

## Request Fields
| Field | Required | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | yes | Model name or alias, e.g. `jev-latest` |
| `state` | yes | A string, object, or array. Every question refers to this content. |
| `questions` | yes | An object of named questions, with at least 1 |
| `assets` | no | Images keyed by placeholders. Each placeholder in strings is swapped for its image. Requires a vision-language model. |

Example question: `"billing": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is this message about billing?"}`

## Question Types and Limits
- **noul:** A yes/no question. `instructions` and `criteria` (`true`/`false`) are both optional.
- **choice:** `criteria` is required and maps choice names to descriptions, with **1–255** entries.
- **score:** `criteria` is required and is an ordered array of **1–10** levels. Scoring starts at 0.
- **box:** Locates something in an image. Requires the Images header.

**Not in the document:**
- A maximum number of questions per request. Only a minimum of 1 is specified.
- A maximum state size or token limit.

## Response
The response has three top-level fields:
- `model`, which may differ from the alias you sent
- `answers`, keyed by your question names
- `usage`, e.g. `{"input_tokens": 120, "output_tokens": 12}`. Output tokens are "currently free of charge."

### noul
Returns a probability of yes/true between 0 and 1.

`"billing": {"type": "noul", "noul": 0.98}`

### choice
Returns `choice` (the option with the highest probability), `confidence`, and `probabilities`. The probabilities sum to roughly 1.

- `"choice": "calm", "confidence": 0.7`
- `"probabilities": {"angry": 0.15, "calm": 0.8, "excited": 0.05}`

### score
Returns `score` (a probability-weighted expected value, which can fall between levels), `confidence`, `legend`, and `probabilities`.

- `"score": 1.7, "confidence": 0.55`
- `{"0": "Can wait", "1": "Needs attention this week", "2": "Needs attention today"}`
- `{"0": 0.1, "1": 0.1, "2": 0.8}`

### box
Returns edges as fractions from 0 to 1, measured from the top and left. `confidence` may be null.

`"box": {"top": 0.2, "bottom": 0.66, "left": 0.19, "right": 0.68}, "confidence": null`

## Errors
- **200:** Success.
- **422:** Validation error. The `detail[]` array contains `loc`, `msg`, and `type` (required), plus optional `input` and `ctx`.
  - Example: `{"loc": ["body", "state"], "msg": "Field required", "type": "missing"}`
- No other status codes (401, 429, 5xx) are documented.

## Rate Limits
The document does not specify any.

The extra context you supplied describes a different system. Its "four requests per minute" limit does not apply to this API.

So Jev through Not Organic is failing in prod with a provider error, likely because the gateway process is holding stale credentials just like Keenable — this breaks the production review gate and hosted research for Twyne users, while Clairic through Not Organic still works fine. Now I want to check how Jev behaves when called directly.

Oh, I think "use scale" means use Jev's Score primitive (ordered levels) as a scale for evaluation — so the user wants Jev Score and Noul questions replacing or complementing LLM judges in evals, since they're cheaper, faster, and calibrated.

For design, I'm thinking per-note Score questions mirroring the existing note_value judge levels, batched across all notes and the draft in a single call to keep state size manageable.

For other eval tasks: rubric weakness recall becomes a noul question per weakness, giving a calibrated expected recall from summed probabilities; rewrite quality could use ordered Score levels or paired noul checks for "fixes the problem" and "keeps meaning"; and research source grounding fits the citation-check pattern with Choice (supports/contradicts/says_nothing) across top-k snippets. I'm also wondering whether Clairic's typed extraction could help pull structured fields like dates or numbers out of research snippets for evaluation.

Clairic is also part of the app under test itself — persona research tools like `extract` get offered to editors when extraction is available (notorganic mode with linked personas enables it). The room run showed zero research extractions out of fifty notes, meaning editors were offered find_passages/extract tools but mostly didn't use them.

I'm thinking I should add a "research_tools_used" metric to the suite to track whether editors actually use Clairic tools during evals, since that's a concrete way to measure Clairic usage. Given the user's phrasing about using Jev and Clairic in evals with scales, I'm planning to implement an evaluator module that runs the judge through the app's own system-one path.

Actually, calling TypeSafe directly with the skate key is cleaner since it keeps the evaluator independent from the app being tested, rather than sharing failure modes through the app's broken path. For Clairic, I can use the app's extract function through Not Organic for the local target, though the live target case still needs sorting out since direct access requires a different token.

For live runs without an in-process app, I'm considering replicating Twyne's extraction call path—checking how the eval client issues tokens and hits the extraction endpoint so I can build an equivalent direct call. Now I'm sketching the evaluator interface structure.

For modes, Jev defaults to direct TypeSafe calls when an API key is present, with an option to route through Not Organic once the gateway's fixed, while Clairic goes through Not Organic using the eval DID since that path already works. Then I'd add scoring hooks for when an evaluator is actually configured.

I realize precision currently unfairly penalizes unlisted-but-legitimate claims, so having Jev judge each returned target's legitimacy for a `jev_target_precision` metric fixes that scoring gap. For Clairic, I'm thinking about matching typed values (statistics, dates) between gold facts and snippets—extracting the fact's key value and comparing it against values pulled from each snippet, though I need to figure out whether to call Clairic per-snippet or bundle everything into one state.

Since Clairic caps fields at twelve per request, I can do one call with the fact plus five labeled snippets, extracting `fact_value` and `source1_value` through `source5_value`, then comparing the normalized values deterministically—a clean typed cross-check. For the interview case, I'm considering having Clairic extract the seven dossier fields from the writer's messages and comparing against the interviewer's DOSSIER fields, but that's comparing two extractions against each other, so I'll set it aside to keep scope tight. I also just hit an important finding: Jev routed through Not Organic is broken.

Tracing through the code, I confirm hosted auto-research is genuinely broken in production right now — the gateway's old TypeSafe key causes the transport to fail, which cascades through askJudgement into a thrown error, meaning both Twyne's review gate and hosted auto-research claim confirmation fail with "the claim check could not run." Keenable has the same root cause, and the fix requires a gateway rebuild the user already chose not to deploy, so I need to flag this clearly as a significant production issue, and note that research.targets hosted strategy cases in evals will error out for the same reason.

I'm also realizing there's no clean workaround for running the eval locally — forcing a notorganic model forces System One into Not Organic routing, and judgementTransport always prefers Not Organic whenever it's enabled, so there's no way to bypass it for a direct Jev path without faking the gateway, which would be too hacky to justify.

I think the honest conclusion is that this hosted research strategy would genuinely fail under these conditions, and that's a real finding rather than an eval artifact. If I wanted to measure quality assuming the gateway gets fixed, I'd need a small, explicit production knob — like an environment override that lets operators force direct transport instead of changing the default precedence logic itself.

Actually, since the model strategy doesn't matter for measuring hosted-strategy quality, I could run with a mock model and the real direct Jev — that isolates hosted strategy with its actual non-LLM behavior, while the model-strategy results in that same run become meaningless and should be filtered out by case name.

But matching exact case ids is limiting, so I'm thinking about whether I need a cleaner way to filter by strategy — maybe adding a runner flag that lets the research-targets suite know which strategy to focus on, rather than hacking around the existing case-id matching.

With this growing in scope, I'm pausing to prioritize: the Keenable bridge is done, next is wiring the Jev evaluator (direct TypeSafe) into suites as additional scores, then a Clairic evaluator via Not Organic for research-source value matching.

Realistically, Clairic should go through app.extract locally since Not Organic already works for eval DID writes there, but for the live target I'll just skip Clairic metrics rather than fight it. I still need to add the --strategy filter for research-targets and document the production finding that Jev via Not Organic is broken, which cascades into the review gate and hosted auto-research.

Let me quickly check on Sol and Astra before diving into the Jev evaluator, and I need to look at how score question criteria are expressed in Twyne's questionValidator -- for score types it's an array of levels, while choice criteria in the TypeSafe API maps option names to descriptions as an object.

Writing Jev interface...

Also designing a groundedness check asking whether each note's text actually responds to what its quote says in the draft, rather than misreading or generic advice, against state with draft and notes. For the rubric, I'm adding per-weakness recall questions that check if feedback substantively identifies each weakness, averaged into an expected recall score, plus a groundedness check for review. For the rewrite judgment, I'm defining "improves" score levels ranging from making the passage worse up through fixing the stated problem in the writer's own voice.

For research-sources evaluation, I'm defining a citation-check pattern where each of the top 5 sources gets rated as supporting, contradicting, or saying nothing about the fact, then combining these into settles and supports scores. I need to work out the logic carefully for planted-error cases, since the fact is always the true statement and sources should be judged against it—supporting the fact effectively contradicts the (wrong) draft passage.

For research-targets, I'm designing a question that checks whether each target's anchor text asserts something a careful reader would expect a source for, rather than opinion or personal experience. I realize this is circular for the hosted strategy since it uses the same criterion, but it's a genuine independent check for the model strategy, so I'm considering phrasing it as a stricter precision check.

Then I'm adding a separate query-quality dimension: checking whether the generated search query would actually find a source capable of verifying the anchor claim, giving two distinct metrics — target precision and query quality.

Now I'm thinking about how to verify factual claims involving statistics or dates, trying to design a field that extracts the specific figure, date, or name asserted by a claim, but running into the problem that the evaluator takes a single state string, so pulling values from both the claim and its sources requires careful handling of which field the instructions refer to.

I should also think through cost implications: Jev calls are cheap since output tokens are free and input is billed directly through TypeSafe on the user's key, while Clairic goes through Not Organic and bills the eval wallet. For Clairic I'd need the in-process extraction path via Not Organic, which only works when the notorganic model is enabled — in mock mode without direct Cloudflare creds, extraction transport is unavailable so Clairic metrics get skipped entirely.

I'm sketching out the ScoreContext interface with optional jev and extract fields, and figuring out the runner defaults — Jev defaults to none under mock models and direct otherwise if a key exists, while Clairic defaults to app mode only when using the notorganic model. Before going further I want to check Sol and Astra's statuses to see if the research ops have landed, since that affects how I test this.

Clairic works through Not Organic, but Jev fails there (same stale-process issue affecting the gateway, though direct Jev calls work fine with the TypeSafe key) — so I'll build the evaluator using Jev directly. Checking Sol and Astra next before setting up the Jev/Clairic evaluators.

With research runs going now, I estimate only about $3-4 spent of the $32.50 total, leaving plenty of room. Beyond just adding cases, I'm considering adding a `--trials N` option to run each case multiple times and capture model variance, aggregating per-case means for Arize (since multiple runs per example may not be well supported) while keeping per-trial detail in the local report. I also want to add confidence intervals to the report — mean ± 95% CI per metric — plus a `compare` command that diffs two reports by case_id with paired significance testing, which is what would make the eval results properly trustworthy.

On concurrency, I ran sequential before to be safe with rate limits, but since each case has its own writer, I think bumping concurrency up to 4 could speed things up without issue. I'm also thinking about generating corpus at scale with Astra plus validators, though real drafts beat synthetic augmentation. Separately, I'm trying to parse what the user meant by "let's use scale our evals" — possibly referencing Scale AI's evaluation platform rather than just scaling up volume, and also noting their mention of a "keenable key" issue with Not Organic that apparently isn't set up properly.

model judges, running 10x more cases for the same budget. The scale plan: have Astra expand the corpus with more cases, and add `--trials N` with confidence intervals for statistical rigor.

APPEND only (never rewrite or reorder existing lines):
- `research.jsonl`: add 16 drafts of about 1,000 words each, same schema and rules as yours.
  - Every flagged claim is real, well documented and searchable, with exact wording for quotes.
  - Include 2 more fiction-on-real-history pieces, 2 more near-empty personal essays (restraint), and 3 drafts with one planted error each.
  - Cover kinds the hosted rule-based strategy misses (works, people in context, unattributed claims) as well as the ones it catches.
- `rewrite.jsonl`: add 16 cases, same schema as the existing 8. Spread them across all five editors and both levels. Include at least 6 passages whose problem tempts a rewriter to drop a fact: a term of art, a number, a place, a proper name. `mustPreserve` lists those exact facts.
- `dossier.jsonl`: add 8 cases, same schema. Mix the drift types and include 2 drafts that drift on nothing, with an empty `drifts` list, to test false alarms.

Validate all old and new lines with your /tmp script, extended to the other two files (word counts, verbatim-once passages, needles inside passages, `mustPreserve` inside `original`, unique ids, original lines byte-identical). Touch only those three files plus a line or two in `evals/app/cases/README.md`. Other agents work in this checkout, so run no state-changing git. Report the validation output and counts.

content.thinking:
Same issue again: the lengthy fact-check prompt demanding exhaustive deliberation over up to 12 claims causes the balanced model to burn through its entire reasoning budget without producing output. Since this will likely repeat across all model cases, three consecutive provider failures should trigger the stop guard.

Actually, I realize hosted cases succeed in between model cases, so the consecutive-failure counter resets each time—meaning the run keeps going but wastes money on repeated failed reasoning calls. I should stop the run now and fix the model strategy before re-running: the root cause is likely that with no output ceiling set, the provider falls back to its own default max_tokens, which gets consumed entirely by reasoning before any answer tokens are generated.

I'm weighing two fixes—explicitly setting a generous output ceiling (12k-16k tokens) so reasoning has room without truncating the answer, versus lowering the reasoning effort for this task since it's really just structured extraction and doesn't need heavy reasoning, though I'm unsure whether the provider actually passes a reasoning_effort parameter through to the upstream model.

I'm also considering whether to just use the lighter "fast" model alias for extraction, since it's structured work and a fast model might handle it reliably even if quality drops slightly, versus splitting the extraction task into smaller pieces to fit within tighter budgets.

So raising maxOutputTokens to something like 16384 would give the model more room to think before answering, and the extra cost at balanced-tier pricing would be negligible—maybe a few cents for a 16k-token reasoning burst. I recall the rationale for not setting an output ceiling was to avoid cutting off responses prematurely.

I'm leaning toward scoping this fix narrowly to research extraction rather than changing it app-wide, since the judges already finish well within the default limit. That means adding an optional maxOutputTokens parameter to the second-chance generation path, since it currently hardcodes the no-ceiling value internally.

Let me check the model docs to see what "balanced" means and whether reasoning_effort is supported there.

The research-extract prompt fails the same way as the judges—`balanced` runs out of tokens (~18k chars) before answering, so every model-strategy case will fail. I'm stopping the run and checking what's behind the alias to figure out the right fix.

/**
 * Twyne sets no output ceiling.
 *
 * These call sites used to carry per-feature budgets — 380 tokens for a note,
 * 200 for a judge — sized against how long the visible answer ought to run.
 * On a model that thinks before it answers the budget is spent on the thinking
 * too, and when it runs out mid-thought the answer never arrives: the reply
 * strips to nothing and a template is filed in its place. Nothing about that
 * looks like a failure to the writer.
 *
 * The ceiling was never what kept an answer short — the prompts do that — so
 * leaving it unset costs nothing. Each provider falls back to its own model
 * maximum, and generation is billed on what a model writes rather than on what
 * it was permitted to write.
 */
const NO_OUTPUT_CEILING = undefined;
input.new_string:
/**
 * Twyne gives every hosted call a generous output ceiling.
 *
 * These call sites used to carry per-feature budgets — 380 tokens for a note,
 * 200 for a judge — sized against how long the visible answer ought to run.
 * On a model that thinks before it answers the budget is spent on the thinking
 * too, and when it runs out mid-thought the answer never arrives: the reply
 * strips to nothing and a template is filed in its place. Nothing about that
 * looks like a failure to the writer.
 *
 * Leaving the ceiling unset did not fix that. It was meant to let each provider
 * fall back to its model maximum, but Not Organic falls back to a default near

 *
 * The prompts are still what keep an answer short; this is headroom, and
 * generation is billed on what a model writes rather than on what it was
 * permitted to write. The name is kept for its many call sites.
 */
export const NO_OUTPUT_CEILING = 16_000;

Another strong candidate is extending Jev/Clairic coverage beyond room and research-sources into rubric, rewrite, dossier, and interview suites, paired with statistical tooling like a compare command for diffing reports with significance testing and Jev-vs-judge calibration analysis — though this risks overlapping with my own planned work.

I should carve out clean file ownership to avoid collisions: I'll hand the Opus agent the suite files for rubric, rewrite, dossier, and interview plus additions to judges.ts and a new stats module for run.ts, while I keep research.ts and any Convex fixes, and Astra owns the corpora. The shared touchpoints in run.ts and judges.ts are the real conflict risk I need to manage carefully.

For spinning up Opus at max effort, I'm weighing whether to use delegate_task with the claude-opus-5-5 model, or the native Agent tool which lets me set model "opus" with an explicit effort parameter -- since the user specifically asked for "opus max," I should set effort to max directly.

Native agents run in the background and report back, sharing the same checkout and tools, and are visible in the Claude Code UI much like T3 delegates are visible there. Since the native Agent tool's model enum supports "opus" with effort "max", and the guidance says to prefer native subagents when they support the chosen model, I'll go with native Agent using model "opus" and effort "max".

For the lane itself, I'm thinking the Opus agent should focus on making the evals trustworthy at scale—building out Jev and Clairic evaluators for rubric, rewrite, dossier, and interview suites, designing calibrated questions grounded in the live TypeSafe docs, while avoiding overlap with the room and research-sources suites I've already built.

I should also bake in statistical rigor: per-metric confidence intervals in summaries, a comparison mode that pairs two runs by case_id and flags significant regressions, and judge-agreement analysis to figure out which evaluators (Jev, LLM judge, deterministic) can actually be trusted. Adding a repeat flag would let me measure run-to-run variance for stochastic models, which fits the "scale" goal, and I want the runner to support higher concurrency safely while respecting rate limits and budget.

Files in scope are the judges, run, and suite files plus a new stats module and README update, while leaving research.ts, room.ts, corpora, convex, and packages untouched since those belong to others. I also need to think about cost — real evals aren't free, and I'm tracking spend against the Not Organic eval wallet, which started around $32.50 and has maybe $5-6 spent across the full run, the fixed run, the judge fix, and the research run. I should give the Opus agent a small budget, maybe capping real verification runs at $3 total, using the provided environment setup.

I'm noting that credential retrieval for this work would use the same production env commands I've already been running myself, so it should be fine as long as the agent never prints secret values, and I should remind it not to run the full test suite — only targeted runs. There's also ambiguity about what "this" refers to in the user's instruction to spin up an Opus subagent — it could mean just the research targets suite I was reporting on, or the eval work more broadly — so I'll interpret it broadly and assign the agent the remaining suites plus scale and statistics work, which seems like the safest, most useful interpretation.

Given that the user prefers giving capable agents loose instructions and letting them run autonomously, I shouldn't second-guess this — I'll just spawn it. But first I need to compile a solid brief for Opus since it's starting cold: key files, how to run things, the credentials recipe, budget constraints, and ownership boundaries, written compactly but completely. I'll also check that the research-sources suite is still running before I spawn the subagent and get back to analyzing results.

input.prompt:
You're joining an eval project for Twyne, a writing app at /home/diogenes/Projects/apps/twyne (Qwik + Convex; branch feat/clairic-extraction). Read `evals/app/README.md` and `docs/app-harness.md` first. Then read `evals/app/run.ts`, `judges.ts`, `scoring.ts`, `local-app.ts` and `suites/*.ts`.

WHAT EXISTS: an eval harness that boots the whole Convex backend in-process (convex-test) and drives Twyne's model features through its real integration API, MCP tools and CLI. There are seven suites (room, rubric, rewrite, dossier, interview, research-targets, research-sources), each with deterministic scorers and optional LLM judges. Results upload to Arize as experiments. It runs on a scripted mock model (free) or on Not Organic, the real hosted gateway, billed to an eval account. Real-run reports from today are in `reports/app-evals/*.json` (prefixes `notorganic-full-20261023`, `notorganic-fixed-20261023`, `research-20261023`).

The user wants two things from your lane:

1. **Jev and Clairic as evaluators across the eval suites.**
   - Jev (TypeSafe's System One model) gives calibrated typed judgements: noul (probability), score (expected value over described levels, with confidence), and choice.
   - Clairic gives typed extraction (text, number, date, list…) with confidence and p_null.
   - Both are already wired as `ScoreContext.jev` / `ScoreContext.extract`, reached through the app's own System One and extraction paths (`LocalApp.judge` / `LocalApp.extract`), and enabled by `--jev`. See `askJev`, `readJevAnswer`, `JEV_NOTE_QUESTIONS` in `judges.ts`, how `suites/room.ts` uses Jev, and how `suites/research.ts` uses both (`jevSettles`, `clairicFact`).
   - Do the same, thoughtfully, for rubric, rewrite, dossier and interview. Examples: a Jev Score on whether a rewrite fixes its stated problem while keeping meaning; Clairic extracting the dossier fields from an interview conversation as objective ground truth; Jev per-dimension readings on rubric drafts as an independent check of the app's own judges.
   - Read the live TypeSafe docs before designing questions: https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt; pages are served as markdown by appending `.md` (primitives/score.md, primitives/noul.md, confidence.md, patterns/composite-scoring.md, cookbooks/citation_check.md). Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand alone. Batch a case's questions into one request.

2. **Scale: make results trustworthy enough to compare runs.**
   - Room and rubric metrics currently have about ±0.12 noise at n=10. Astra (another agent) is expanding the corpora in `evals/app/cases/` right now, to about 40 room drafts, 20 rubric pairs, 24 research drafts, 24 rewrites and 12 dossiers.
   - Add per-metric 95% confidence intervals to reports and the printed summary.
   - Add a way to compare two runs (e.g. `--baseline <report.json>`, or a small compare script): paired by case_id, with the delta, its CI, and a flag when a change is beyond noise.
   - Add evaluator agreement (Jev vs the LLM judge vs the deterministic checks, on the cases where all exist), so we learn which evaluators to trust.
   - Optionally `--repeat N` to measure run-to-run variance.
   - Keep the Arize upload working: flat `eval.<name>.score|label|explanation` columns, numeric scores in every row, and text labels that pandas won't coerce to numbers. See `arize.ts` for why.

OWNERSHIP (shared checkout, other agents active, so this matters):
- You own `evals/app/judges.ts`, `evals/app/run.ts`, `evals/app/suites/{rubric,rewrite,dossier,interview}.ts`, `evals/app/scoring.ts`, any new files you add under `evals/app/`, and the README.
- Do NOT edit `evals/app/suites/room.ts`, `evals/app/suites/research.ts`, `evals/app/cases/*` (Astra), anything in `convex/`, `src/`, `prompts/` or `packages/`, or the Not Organic repo.
- If you need an app-side change, describe it in your report rather than making it.
- No state-changing git, no deploys.
- Re-read files right before editing; I may touch research.ts and room.ts meanwhile.

VERIFY:
- `bun test evals/app` (fast, mock model). It must stay green; extend it for what you add.
- Type-check the harness alone: `npx tsc -p /tmp/twyne-probe/tsconfig.evals-app.json`. Never run the repo's full test suite (over 10 minutes) and don't loop on tsc.
- You may spend up to US$3 of real model credit verifying against the real stack, on a few cases at most.

The real-stack env recipe (never print secret values):
```
export NOTORGANIC_ENABLED=true NOTORGANIC_ISSUER="$(npx convex env get --prod NOTORGANIC_ISSUER)" NOTORGANIC_AUDIENCE="$(npx convex env get --prod NOTORGANIC_AUDIENCE)" NOTORGANIC_ASSERTION_PRIVATE_KEY="$(npx convex env get --prod NOTORGANIC_ASSERTION_PRIVATE_KEY)" TWYNE_EVAL_DID="$(skate get twyne-eval-did)" TWYNE_EVAL_SESSION_VERSION=0 TWYNE_EVAL_MAX_COST_MICROUSD=50000000 TYPESAFE_API_KEY="$(skate get typesafe_api_key)" KEENABLE_API_KEY="$(skate get keenable-api-key@secrets)"
bun evals/app/run.ts --suite <s> --case <ids> --model notorganic --system-one direct --research keenable --judge notorganic --jev --concurrency 1 --out /tmp/<dir>
```
Leave out `--arize` so test runs don't clutter Arize. `--system-one direct` is needed because Not Organic's own System One route currently fails; Jev goes direct with the same key the gateway uses.

Report back:
- files changed;
- the Jev/Clairic questions you designed and why;
- what the statistics show on today's existing reports (CIs per suite, and agreement between evaluators where the data allows);
- test and type-check results;
- anything you'd change in the app.

Real-run reports from today are in `reports/app-evals/*.json` (prefixes `notorganic-full-20261023`, `notorganic-fixed-20261023`, `research-20261023`).

The user wants two things from your lane:

1. **Jev and Clairic as evaluators across the eval suites.**
   - Jev (TypeSafe's System One model) gives calibrated typed judgements: noul (probability), score (expected value over described levels, with confidence), and choice.
   - Clairic gives typed extraction (text, number, date, list…) with confidence and p_null.
   - Both are already wired as `ScoreContext.jev` / `ScoreContext.extract`, reached through the app's own System One and extraction paths (`LocalApp.judge` / `LocalApp.extract`), and enabled by `--jev`. See `askJev`, `readJevAnswer`, `JEV_NOTE_QUESTIONS` in `judges.ts`, how `suites/room.ts` uses Jev, and how `suites/research.ts` uses both (`jevSettles`, `clairicFact`).
   - Do the same, thoughtfully, for rubric, rewrite, dossier and interview. Examples: a Jev Score on whether a rewrite fixes its stated problem while keeping meaning; Clairic extracting the dossier fields from an interview conversation as objective ground truth; Jev per-dimension readings on rubric drafts as an independent check of the app's own judges.
   - Read the live TypeSafe docs before designing questions: https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt; pages are served as markdown by appending `.md` (primitives/score.md, primitives/noul.md, confidence.md, patterns/composite-scoring.md, cookbooks/citation_check.md). Score levels must describe concrete situations and stand alone. Batch a case's questions into one request.

2. **Scale: make results trustworthy enough to compare runs.**
   - Room and rubric metrics currently have about ±0.12 noise at n=10. Astra (another agent) is expanding the corpora in `evals/app/cases/` right now, to about 40 room drafts, 20 rubric pairs, 24 research drafts, 24 rewrites and 12 dossiers.
   - Add per-metric 95% confidence intervals to reports and the printed summary.
   - Add a way to compare two runs (e.g. `--baseline <report.json>`, or a small compare script): paired by case_id, with the delta, its CI, and a flag when a change is beyond noise.
   - Add evaluator agreement (Jev vs the LLM judge vs the deterministic checks, on the cases where all exist), so we learn which evaluators to trust.
   - Optionally `--repeat N` to measure run-to-run variance.
   - Keep the Arize upload working: flat `eval.<name>.score|label|explanation` columns, numeric scores in every row, and text labels that pandas won't coerce to numbers. See `arize.ts` for why.

| | **hosted** (rules + Jev, what hosted writers get today) | **model** (extraction prompts on the hosted model) |
|---|---|---|
| Claims needing a source that got flagged | **0.40** | **1.00** |
| Left opinion/experience alone | 1.00 | 0.91 |

| Planted errors flagged | 1/1 | 1/1 |

Hosted writers' auto-research misses 60% of the claims that need sources: on the history and web drafts it found 0–17%. The model strategy found every one, at the cost of slight over-flagging: a metaphor and two personal details in the restraint essay. It cost about 1.4¢ per draft. The sources suite (42 claims through Keenable, judged by the LLM, Jev and Clairic) is running now.

content.thinking:
I realize my fact-checking comparison is flawed—comparing a precise extracted value like "5.145°" against a vague prose fact like "about five degrees" fails string matching, and claims lacking a specific value end up mismatched against unrelated data like dates. A better approach would be to extract the same typed field from both the fact and the sources, then compare those typed values directly rather than relying on string comparison.

I should determine field type based on claim kind: statistics map to numbers, events to dates, and other claim types might skip numeric comparison entirely, instead measuring whether the sources state anything at all about the claim. I can run the same extraction instructions on both the fact text and the sources to get comparable values, then compare numbers with a tolerance and dates by precision, while for text-based claims I'd just measure "stated" vs "not stated" based on whether a null value was returned.

The expected_source metric at 0.50 is actually too strict since it only checks for specific named domains, while the LLM judge and the other evaluator both show much higher settlement rates — that metric is really measuring "named authority present" rather than true settlement, so I should keep it but label it accurately. I'm also noting both evaluators agree almost universally that these corpus facts are settled, which suggests the test corpus of encyclopedic facts might be too easy compared to real writer claims — a good future improvement, but not urgent now. Time to actually implement the typed field approach in clairicFact.

I'm defining sets for numeric and date claim kinds, then writing a scoring function that maps claim kind to an expected value type — returning a null score with a "n/a" label when there's no single typed value to compare for text-based claims. I'm weighing whether null scores causing label-only treatment in the upload pipeline is acceptable, and now I want to check how many "event" claims actually contain extractable dates in the corpus before finalizing this.

Instead of relying purely on claim kind, I'm considering deriving the comparison type from the fact text itself: a year-like token suggests a date field, a plain number suggests a numeric field, otherwise it's n/a. The plan is to run the same field extraction on both the fact and the sources, then compare typed values — for numbers, allowing a relative or absolute tolerance, and for dates, comparing at whatever precision is available (year-only vs full date).

For the comparison I'll compute the common prefix length using the shorter string, and treat a null value as "not stated." Each case needs two extraction calls, which is a minor cost, and I don't think a reference date is necessary here. I also want to tweak the README wording around expected_source to say "a corpus-named authority appears" instead of "settles," and I'm thinking about whether I can re-score existing raw results offline or whether I need to re-run everything live through the extraction tool.

Given the Arize experiment already uploaded with the broken clairic_fact, I think the cleanest path is deleting the old run and re-running the research-sources suite with the same experiment name — the cost is small, around $0.30. Since I'll be running everything again anyway once the corpus expansion lands, for now I'll just fix the issue and verify it on a smaller scale.

Cost estimate is about $0.35, which is fine. Time to write the fix.

I found two scoring bugs: the Clairic check compares extracted values as raw strings (missing equivalent values like "5.145°" vs "about five degrees"), and `expected_source` only matches against a fixed domain list, flagging correct but unlisted sources as misses. I'll fix the Clairic check by extracting typed values from both fact and sources and comparing them numerically/as dates.

content.thinking:
Now that the research, rewrite, and dossier corpora are scaled, I want to spot-check the new research corpus for factual accuracy before running anything, since structure validation doesn't guarantee truth—I should sample some facts and verify a few planted errors. I'm also noting that the dossier suite has two zero-drift controls where the recall ratio would compute as null, so I need to check how the dossier scorer handles that edge case.

For zero-drift controls, a null score would upload as label-only in Arize, which isn't quite right—I think the better fix is adding a false-alarm metric that checks whether the detector flagged anything when it shouldn't have, since that's the whole point of these controls. But I don't own dossier.ts since I delegated that suite ownership to the Opus subagent, so instead of editing it myself I should message that agent to add the false-alarm metric.

The rewrite cases with exact-fact preservation look fine with the existing scorer. For my own research suite, I'm working through how the targets scorer handles the two zero-flag essays—recall defaults to 1 when there are no required flags, and precision should be 0 if the model flags anything on an essay that shouldn't be flagged at all, which the restraint metric already covers. That logic seems reasonable.

Now I'm estimating costs: the sources suite runs one case per gold claim, and with roughly 138 claims across search, judge, and Clairic calls, that's probably around $0.60 total. The targets suite at 48 cases should run about $0.35. Trying to tally total spend so far against the $30+$2.50 budget—the wallet view is broken since the portal fix isn't deployed, so I'm reconstructing it from per-suite billing logs instead: room, rubric, rewrite, and interview costs from the earlier fixed run, plus the judge-fix and research suite costs, adding up to a modest fraction of the budget.

I'm confirming that the billed() usage call captures everything under the same DID within the time window, including judge calls through the eval client, so the accounting should be complete and well under the $30 cap.

Now I want to spot-check a sample of the new research claims for factual accuracy, since a wrong "fact" would unfairly penalize correct sources during evaluation—so I'm pulling up the new drafts list and planted errors to verify a handful against what I know.

The research, rewrite, and dossier steps now scale to all 60 cases and pass structural validation. Before proceeding, I'll spot-check the new research facts for accuracy, since structural validation alone wouldn't catch a false "fact" that could unfairly penalize correct sources.

The factual-error plants in fictional drafts look good as internal inconsistencies for the scholar to catch. The "legal-review-window" rubric pair also works well, with the weak draft being a subtly fluent but legally incorrect version I'm designing as a plant.

While waiting on the Opus subagent, I'm estimating costs for the full scaled run: room (45 cases), rubric pairs (32), rewrite (24), dossier (12), interview (10), research-targets (48), and research-sources (126) — a lot of model calls. I'm trying to reconcile the billing figures, since judge calls appear to be billed to the same eval DID as the app calls, which means the $0.18 figure for the room run likely already includes both the 51 app calls and roughly 34 judge calls, totaling the 85 settled calls reported.

But that math doesn't quite work either — with 50 notes and three judge dimensions (faithful, helpful, value), I'd expect 150 judge calls plus 51 app calls, which is 201 total, not 85. I suspect the usage API caps results at 100 and flags a truncated response, so the billed figure might just be a lower bound I should note or display more clearly as "≥$X (truncated)". For now I'll estimate total spend is a few dollars out of the $30 grant, and a full run with judges should stay comfortably under the $50 cap, though I still need to verify via the portal once my scoped-grant fix is deployed.

I also can't easily sum usage past 100 rows, so I'll just estimate from per-suite billed figures and cap concurrency rather than over-engineer this. Fixing the truncation display in run.ts would help, but that file is now owned by the Opus subagent, so I'll leave it for later. For the room suite, with 45 drafts running through the review gate at roughly $0.018/case, total cost lands around $0.9 plus judge calls, and the research-sources suite with 126 claims will add its own cost on top of that.

Scaling means speed via concurrency too — since each case gets its own writer token, rate limits aren't an issue locally, so concurrency is mainly bounded by the `--concurrency` flag (default 2). I've been running with `--concurrency 1` for safety, but at ~45s per room case sequentially that's ~34 minutes for 45 cases, versus ~9 minutes at concurrency 4 — though I'm unsure how the Not Organic gateway handles rate limits under that load.

Each case already spawns 5 parallel model calls, so concurrency 3 means 15 parallel calls, and the real risk is the reservation ceiling: `balanced` calls reserve $0.50 each but `reasoning` calls reserve $2.00 each, and since rubric judging runs 5 persona judges in parallel via Promise.all, that's $10 reserved per rubric case — at concurrency 3 that's $30 reserved simultaneously, which could exceed the remaining balance and trigger a 402 insufficient_funds error.

I need to keep rubric concurrency at 1-2 to be safe. The cost ceilings come from TWYNE_EVAL_MAX_COST_MICROUSD ($50) interacting with the per-alias ceiling — the effective cap ends up being the alias ceiling itself, $2 for reasoning and $0.50 for balanced, which confirms the reservation pressure I calculated.

For a room test case with 5 balanced persona calls, a System One call, and judges running 3 sequential calls per note across 5 notes concurrently, that's 5 concurrent $2 reservations at once ($10), doubling to $20 at concurrency 2 — uncomfortably close to a $27 balance, so concurrency 1 is the safer choice.

Let me tally today's spend more carefully — rough estimates across room runs, rubric failures, probes, fixes, and judge corrections suggest $3-4 spent so far, leaving roughly $28 of the $32.50 balance. Scaling the full run to about 4.5x the cases would put room costs (with judges) around $2-3, with rubric pairs adding more on top.

I'm now sizing the rest: rewrite, dossier, interview, research targets, and sources together land around $5-8 total for the scaled run, which seems manageable.

I also notice the usage API only returns up to 100 records before truncating, so per-suite spend tracking isn't fully accurate — fixing that would mean adding pagination logic on the app side, which isn't worth doing right now; I'll just flag it. While waiting on the Opus agent, I'm also weighing whether to drop the faithfulness/helpfulness judges at scale since they pass near 100% anyway, keeping only the more discriminating note-value judge to cut costs.

But since those judges mirror Arize's rubrics, I'll keep them for now and let the Opus agent's agreement analysis tell me which ones are actually worth retaining. I shouldn't poll for its completion, so I'll just prep the full-run command and cost guard in the meantime, and consider checking Arize's experiment list for cleanup. One loose end worth capturing in memory: the Keenable deployment has the correct gateway key but predates the fix, can't be redeployed without a new build — that's a durable fact worth saving.

I should also note why Not Organic's System One route fails for the eval DID (same key-mismatch story, needs --system-one direct), and record the actual secret locations — keenable-api-key@secrets and typesafe_api_key — since they match the gateway's values. This explains the user's earlier confusion about why the keenable key setup wasn't working: the key is correctly set, but the live deployment predates the rotation, so Railway won't let it redeploy without a fresh build, which is why the eval bridge was chosen instead.

Now I'm realizing the root cause is broader: TypeSafe, Keenable, and FAL credentials were all rotated, but the running gateway still has the old ones loaded, which explains why Jev via Not Organic fails with a "provider" error — same issue as before. Clairic worked fine because it uses a separate Cloudflare AI token untouched by the rotation. This means in production right now, all of Twyne's hosted System One features — the review gate, hosted research claim confirmation, and persona research judge — are silently broken until a new build loads the staged credentials, which is a serious issue since the editorial review gate would pass everything unreviewed without any judgment ever withholding a note.

This is a bigger deal than I initially thought: hosted auto-research entirely fails in production, meaning the claim check throws and hosted writers currently get no auto-research at all. The user had decided to skip the gateway rebuild, but they made that call only knowing about the Keenable issue — now that I've confirmed Jev/TypeSafe is also broken through the same stale deployment, I should surface this clearly in my summary so they can reconsider. Before asserting this though, I want to double-check how systemOne's askNotOrganic maps provider errors, since a non-429/402 failure status gets bucketed as "provider."

I should probe the gateway's system-one endpoint directly to confirm this is a 5xx upstream error from a stale key rather than something related to the eval DID's permissions or session version — inference and extraction already worked with that DID, so session isn't the issue. I also want to flag that two uncommitted fixes in the notorganic-provider repo (the $0 portal display and the session_revoked 401 mapping) would ship automatically if the user rebuilds from the working tree, though that tree has dozens of other uncommitted files mixed in. Let me run the probe now.

While waiting on the Opus lane, I'm investigating why Jev failed through Not Organic but Clairic succeeded—likely the gateway's stale TypeSafe key rather than our request, which could mean production is affected too.

I spent about $0.60 checking it against the real stack.

## Files changed
- **Edited:** `judges.ts`, `run.ts`, `scoring.ts`, `suites/{rubric,rewrite,dossier,interview}.ts`, `README.md`.
- **New:** `stats.ts`, `agreement.ts`, `reports.ts`, `compare.ts`, `stats.test.ts`, `evaluators.test.ts`.
- **Untouched:** room.ts, research.ts, the cases, local-app.ts, types.ts, and everything under convex/src/prompts/packages.
- **Behaviour changes worth knowing:**
  - A garbled `weakness_recall` reply is now `judge-error`; before, it silently scored 0.
  - Dossier gains a deterministic `field_precision`.
  - `drift_recall` scores 1 ("nothing to find") on the new aligned cases, so it stays a number for Arize.
  - Rubric pair-order scores now count once per pair in the statistics.

## Questions designed, and why
Each case's questions go in one request. I made one exception: a reading meant to be independent never shares state with the app's verdicts or the corpus's answers, because Jev reads the whole state for every question.

- **Rubric:**
  - Four blind Scores (sufficiency, evidence, integrity, target fit), on the draft and brief only. Their four levels copy the app judges' own anchors (scores 1, 4, 7, 10), so the two compare directly.
  - These combine into `jev_quality` (equal weights) and a Jev pair order.
  - For weak drafts, a second request asks one Noul per planted weakness: the same question the LLM judge answers, so the two can be compared weakness by weakness.
- **Rewrite:**
  - Scores for how much of the stated problem is left, and how much of the original's meaning survives.
  - Nouls for "adds a figure, date, name, event, study or source the draft doesn't mention" and "still fits where the original stood".
  - One Noul per fact the corpus says must survive.
  - `jev_rewrite` = 0.5 fix + 0.3 meaning + 0.2 fit.
  - On real rewrites plus copies with a planted fake study, source or figure, the invention question read 0.02–0.29 on genuine and 0.90–0.98 on planted. An earlier wording mistook a paraphrase for an invention.
- **Dossier:**
  - Blind to the planted drifts: is each observation actually true of the draft?

-{"case_id": "dossier-register-kids-moon", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Why Does the Moon Follow the Car?", "format": "feature for a children's science magazine", "audience": "readers aged nine to eleven, reading alone", "goal": "explain why the moon seems to follow you and why it looks bigger near the horizon, so a ten-year-old can explain it to a parent", "tone": "playful, direct, second person, short sentences", "constraints": "under 700 words; no word a ten-year-old would have to look up; no equations", "successSignal": "a ten-year-old can explain the trick to a grown-up with their hands"}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "You are in the back of the car at night, and the moon is following you. You go past a row of houses and it is still there, over the roofs. You go round a corner and it comes too. The trees whip past, the lamp posts whip past, and the moon just hangs there, keeping up, as if it has nothing better to do.

It is not following you. It only looks that way, and the reason is one of the best tricks your eyes play on you.

Here is the trick. Hold your thumb up at arm's length and look at it with one eye, then the other. It jumps. Now look at something across the room and do the same thing. It jumps less. Now look out of the window at the furthest thing you can see. It barely moves at all. The further away something is, the less it seems to move when you move. The moon is very, very far away, so far that when the car goes a whole mile, the moon has moved, from your point of view, by nothing you could notice. The houses are close, so they rush past. The moon is far, so it stays. That is the whole trick.

The apparent angular displacement of a distant object under lateral translation of the observer is inversely proportional to its distance, a phenomenon generally termed motion parallax, and the lunar case represents the limiting condition in which the parallax angle approaches zero.

The moon does something else that is strange, and this one even grown-ups argue about. When it is low down, just coming up over the houses, it looks huge. An hour later, high in the sky, it looks small. If you hold out your thumb and cover it, you will find your thumb covers it both times, exactly the same. It has not changed size. Your brain has changed its mind about how big it is.

Nobody is completely sure why. The best guess is this. When the moon is low, you see it next to things you know the size of: houses, trees, a church. Your brain says, that is as big as a house, and that is far away, so it must be enormous. When the moon is high, there is nothing next to it, just sky, and your brain has nothing to compare it with, so it decides the moon is small. Same moon. Different neighbours.

Contemporary accounts invoke a conjunction of the Ponzo illusion and size-distance invariance, though the literature remains unsettled, and it is doubtful that any single explanatory model will prove adequate to the full phenomenology of the effect.

You can test this. Next time the moon is low and looks huge, bend over and look at it upside down between your legs. It will look smaller. Nothing has changed except that your brain can no longer line it up with the houses, so it stops pretending.

So here is what to tell the grown-up in the front seat. Hold up your thumb. Close one eye, then the other. Show them how the thumb jumps and the far-off thing does not. Then tell them the moon is the furthest-off thing there is, so it does not jump at all, which is why it seems to keep up with the car. Then, if the moon is low, tell them to bend over and look at it upside down. They will not want to. Make them. It works.

The moon is about two hundred and forty thousand miles away. That is so far that if you drove there at motorway speed, without stopping, it would take you about five months. The car has gone one mile. The moon has noticed nothing. It is not following you. It is just too far away to be left behind.

And one more thing for the ride home. The stars do the same trick, and they are so much further away that they do not even seem to move when the whole planet turns underneath them for an hour. The moon follows the car. The stars follow the moon. -{"case_id": "dossier-goal-compost-pilot", "brief": {"answers": {"workingTitle": "Join the Harbour Ward Compost Pilot", "format": "email to residents from the council's waste team", "audience": "residents of the four hundred households in the Harbour Ward pilot area", "goal": "get at least a hundred households to sign up for the food-waste collection pilot before the Friday deadline", "tone": "friendly, brisk, clear about what to do", "constraints": "under 600 words; the sign-up link and the Friday deadline must appear in the first paragraph and again at the end", "successSignal": "a resident knows what the pilot is, what they get, and clicks the link before Friday"}, "attachments": [], "completedAt": 1790000000000, "updatedAt": 1790000000000}, "draftText": "Dear neighbour,

For as long as there has been a Harbour Ward, there has been a question about what to do with the food we do not eat. The ward's first refuse collection began in 1894, with a horse-drawn cart and two men who were paid in part with the right to sell what they collected. Kitchen scraps went to pig keepers on the edge of town, and for sixty years that arrangement, informal as it was, meant that very little of the ward's food waste ended up in the ground.

That changed in the 1950s, when the pig keepers were moved out and the council introduced the bins most of us still use. Since then, almost all food waste in the ward has gone to landfill, where it breaks down without air and produces methane, a gas that warms the planet many times more effectively than carbon dioxide. The council's most recent waste audit found that food makes up roughly a third of what goes into the average Harbour Ward bin by weight.

Across the country, councils have begun separating food waste for collection, and the results have been encouraging. Food collected separately can be processed in sealed digesters that capture the methane and burn it for electricity, and what remains can be spread on farmland. The ward's waste team has been studying these schemes for two years, visiting four other councils and reviewing the costs, and we have come to the view that a separate food-waste collection would work here.

We are therefore running a pilot. Four hundred households in the streets between the harbour and the railway line, including yours, have been selected. Households that take part will receive a small lidded caddy for the kitchen, a supply of compostable liners, and a larger outdoor bin, and the food waste will be collected weekly, on the same day as the recycling. The caddy is designed to sit on a worktop or under a sink, and in the councils we visited, residents reported that it did not smell if the liner was changed every two or three days.

We know that some residents will have questions. Some will worry about smells, or about attracting animals, or about the extra bin taking up space in a small yard. The waste team has thought about each of these and has answers that we will share as the pilot goes on. Some residents will also, reasonably, want to know what happens after the pilot, and the honest answer is that it depends on what we learn: if enough households take part and the collected waste is clean enough to process, the council will consider extending the scheme to the whole ward in the following year.

The pilot is the first time in seventy years that the ward has tried to do something different with its food waste, and it is, in a small way, a return to the older arrangement, in which the scraps went somewhere useful rather than into the ground. We are grateful to the residents' association for its help in selecting the pilot streets and to the four councils whose experience we have drawn on.

There will be more to say about this in the months ahead, and we will write again once the pilot is under way with details of collection days and what can and cannot go in the caddy. In the meantime, the waste team can be reached through the council's main switchboard during office hours.

With best wishes,
